Best Synology Alternatives in 2026 | Starry Hope Starry Hope 
 The Best Synology Alternatives in 2026
Updated on
 November 2, 2026,
by Jim Mendenhall 
 Bottom line 
 UGREEN’s NASync line is the closest replacement for a Synology NAS. Its boxes run a similar all-in-one system on newer hardware with faster network ports. TrueNAS or Unraid on hardware you choose gives you full control of the software. If Synology’s backup apps are why you bought one, staying put still makes sense.
Recommendation
 The four-bay UGREEN DXP4800 Plus pairs 10GbE with Quick Sync video transcoding for Plex. For a TrueNAS or Unraid build, the Minisforum N5 Pro has a 12-core chip, ECC support, and room for virtual machines.
 A Synology alternative can mean three different purchases: another ready-made NAS with its own software, NAS hardware you load with TrueNAS or Unraid, or plain storage with the apps moved somewhere else. In 2026 the main reason to leave is hardware. Synology’s four-bay DS925+ uses a 2018 AMD chip with no video engine, the DS225+ and DS425+ keep a 2019 Celeron with 2GB of memory, and none of the 2025 desktop models has built-in 10GbE. The drive-lock rule that drew the loudest complaints in 2025 now applies mainly to M.2 SSDs.
 UGREEN, TerraMaster, Minisforum, and AOOSTAR prices below are list prices from each maker’s US store in late 2026. Sales move them often.
 Synology alternatives at a glance
 Alternative Type Starting list price Best for 
 UGREEN DXP4800 Plus Ready-made, UGOS Pro $619.99 A direct DiskStation swap with 10GbE and Plex transcoding 
 UGREEN DXP2800 Ready-made, UGOS Pro $389.99 A two-bay replacement for a DS220+ or DS225+ 
 QNAP TS-464 Ready-made, QTS or QuTS hero varies ZFS on a ready-made box, and a PCIe slot 
 TerraMaster F4-425 Plus Ready-made, TOS 7 $599.99 A cheaper four-bay with 5GbE ports 
 UniFi UNAS Pro Storage appliance $499 Seven bays of file storage on a UniFi network 
 Minisforum N5 Pro Open hardware $899 (no RAM) TrueNAS, Unraid, or Proxmox with room for VMs 
 Minisforum N5 Air Open hardware $495 (no RAM) Five bays and 10GbE for a TrueNAS or Unraid build 
 AOOSTAR WTR Pro 5825U Open hardware $379 (no RAM) The cheapest four-bay box for TrueNAS or Unraid 
 UGREEN DXP480T Plus All-SSD, UGOS Pro $899.99 Fast shared storage for video editing over 10GbE or Thunderbolt 
 TrueNAS Community Edition Software Free ZFS storage on hardware you choose 
 Unraid Software $49 to $249 Mixed drive sizes and a large app catalog 
 The UniFi price is from WunderTech’s guide . QNAP’s US street price for the TS-464 changes often and usually sits in the same range as the four-bay UGREEN and TerraMaster boxes. Every model on the NAS comparison chart can be sorted by bays, network speed, and transcoding support.
 What still pushes buyers away from Synology
 The drive lock is mostly gone. When Synology launched the 2025 Plus models, they refused to set up storage on hard drives outside Synology’s own list. After months of complaints, Synology’s DSM 7.3 release on October 8, 2025 restored third-party hard drives and 2.5-inch SATA SSDs on those models. The M.2 slots still take only Synology’s own NVMe SSDs for new storage pools and caches, so a DS925+ owner who wants a cheap Samsung or WD SSD cache cannot add one. WunderTech also notes that Synology has not committed to open drive support on future models, and its UGREEN vs Synology comparison points out that some newer DSM storage features still require Synology drives: “It isn’t fair to say you can use third-party drives, full stop.”
 The DS925+ lists at $700 and carries an AMD Ryzen V1500B from 2018, 4GB of ECC memory, and two 2.5GbE ports with no slot for a faster card. That chip has no graphics engine, so Plex and Jellyfin cannot hardware-transcode video on it. The two-bay DS225+ and four-bay DS425+ use the 2019 Celeron J4125 with 2GB of memory. Synology also removed its own Video Station app in DSM 7.2.2, which left media playback to third-party apps.
 Synology still has the better software. Hyper Backup, Active Backup for Business, Snapshot Replication, and Synology Photos have years of fixes behind them, and DSM 7.3 gets maintenance updates through October 2027 under Synology’s life-cycle policy . Every alternative below gives up some of that, so list the DSM apps you use before you shop.
 UGREEN NASync is the closest DiskStation replacement
 UGREEN NASync DXP4800 Plus
 Editor's Choice 
 4-Bay 10GbE 8GB RAM Intel Pentium Gold 8505 
 List price $619.99 | Full specs 
Check Price on Amazon
 UGREEN NASync DXP2800
 Most Compact 
 2-Bay 2.5GbE 8GB RAM Intel Processor N100 
 List price $389.99 | Full specs 
Check Price on Amazon
 You put drives in a UGREEN NASync box, open a web page, and get a storage pool, file shares, a photo app with face recognition, a sync app, Docker, and virtual machines, all inside UGREEN’s own UGOS Pro, as on a DiskStation. The DXP4800 Plus lists at $619.99 with a 12th-generation Intel Pentium Gold 8505, 8GB of DDR5 that expands to 64GB, a 10GbE port next to a 2.5GbE port, two M.2 slots that take any NVMe SSD, and a separate 128GB system SSD. That is $80 less than the DS925+ for a newer CPU, twice the memory, and four times the network speed on one port.
 Intel’s Quick Sync video engine is in every Intel-based NASync model, so Plex (with a Plex Pass) and Jellyfin can transcode 4K HEVC on the GPU instead of the CPU cores. WunderTech’s alternatives guide makes the same point: “the Intel models handle Plex transcoding that current Synology Plus devices can’t do at all.” For a two-bay swap, the DXP2800 lists at $389.99 with an Intel N100, 8GB of DDR5, and two M.2 slots, though it has a single 2.5GbE port and tops out at 16GB of memory.
 For backups, WunderTech’s UGREEN vs Synology comparison says “on the UGREEN side you’re mostly syncing your data, not backing it up,” because a deletion on the NAS can carry through to the backup copy. UGOS Pro also cannot encrypt a whole volume, only individual shared folders. If you leave UGOS Pro later, you can install TrueNAS or Unraid on the same box; UGREEN has said that a third-party system does not by itself void the hardware warranty, though it will not support the software. Our UGREEN vs Synology comparison covers the model pairs, ECC memory, and the software gap in more detail.
 QNAP adds a PCIe slot and ZFS but runs an older chip
 QNAP’s QTS system has a comparable range of apps, including Hybrid Backup Sync for versioned backups to other devices and the cloud. The four-bay TS-464 has an Intel Celeron N5095 with Quick Sync, 8GB of memory, two 2.5GbE ports, two M.2 slots, and a PCIe slot that takes a 10GbE or faster network card. Neither the DS925+ nor UGREEN’s four-bay boxes have a PCIe slot. QNAP also offers QuTS hero, a ZFS-based version of its system, and the TS-464 can switch to it from QTS 5.2.1 onward. That puts ZFS checksumming and snapshots on a ready-made box with a vendor app store.
 QNAP released the TS-464 in 2022 around Intel’s Celeron N5095, a 2021 chip, so it sits a generation behind UGREEN’s N100 and Pentium Gold models. WunderTech, who runs Synology, UGREEN, and TrueNAS boxes, wrote of QTS : “The operating system is just a lot, and it’s the one I find least pleasant to actually use.” The DeadBolt ransomware encrypted QNAP units exposed to the internet in early 2022, after the Qlocker and eCh0raix campaigns the year before. Keep any NAS, from any maker, off direct internet exposure and reach it through a VPN or a tunnel instead.
 TerraMaster costs less and has rougher software
 TerraMaster F4-425 Plus
 Budget Pick 
 4-Bay 5GbE 8GB RAM Intel Processor N95 
 List price $599.99 | Full specs 
Check Price on Amazon
 The TerraMaster F4-425 Plus N150 model lists at $649.99 with 16GB of DDR5, three M.2 slots, and two 5GbE ports in an aluminum case. A later-released N95 model lists at $599.99 with 8GB of DDR4 and the same ports. Two 5GbE ports are double the speed of the DS925+‘s 2.5GbE, and both the N150 and N95 transcode video with Quick Sync. TerraMaster’s TOS 7 includes TRAID, its version of Synology’s mixed-drive SHR, plus Btrfs snapshots, a photo app, and Docker.
 NASCompares listed the TOS 6 interface and apps as less polished than the top NAS platforms in a review that predates TOS 7, and WunderTech, after praising TOS 6’s backup tools, concluded : “I can’t recommend it as your primary NAS yet.” The F4-425 Plus also has no PCIe slot, so 5GbE is as fast as it goes, and its M.2 slots run at one PCIe 3.0 lane each. TerraMaster does not lock the hardware, so Unraid or TrueNAS can replace TOS if it does not work out.
 UniFi UNAS Pro is storage only
 If your home network already runs on UniFi gear, Ubiquiti’s UNAS Pro is a seven-bay rackmount NAS at $499, with a 10GbE port and 8GB of memory. It runs UniFi Drive, which handles file shares, snapshots, and backups inside the same UniFi console you use for the router and access points. NASCompares’ review found it struggled to hold full 10GbE speed under sustained heavy load.
 The UNAS Pro has no Docker, no Plex, and no photo app. The UNAS Pro makes sense as a Synology replacement only when you pair it with a separate app box, such as a mini PC running Plex and Docker. Our guide to running a mini PC as a home server covers that half.
 Run TrueNAS or Unraid on hardware you pick
 Minisforum N5 Pro
 Best Performance 
 5-Bay 10GbE No RAM AMD Ryzen AI 9 HX PRO 370 
 List price $899.00 | Full specs 
Check Price on Amazon
 AOOSTAR WTR PRO 5825U
 Best Value 
 4-Bay 2.5GbE No RAM AMD Ryzen 7 5825U 
 List price $379.00 | Full specs 
Check Price on Amazon
 A DiskStation runs DSM and nothing else in any supported way, so leaving Synology’s software means leaving its hardware. The alternative is NAS hardware that takes any x86 operating system, loaded with TrueNAS (free) or Unraid (paid).
 TrueNAS Community Edition is free and open source, built on the ZFS file system. iXsystems folded its older CORE and SCALE editions into this one Linux-based release in 2025, and version 25.10 arrived in October 2025. ZFS checksums every block, repairs corrupted data from parity, and can replicate snapshots to a second box on a schedule, which covers much of what Hyper Backup and Snapshot Replication do on Synology. It runs Docker apps from a built-in catalog. ZFS pools work best with matched drives, expanding a pool takes planning, and the interface assumes you know what a vdev (a group of drives with its own redundancy) is.
 Unraid is paid. A Starter license is $49 for up to six storage devices, Unleashed is $109 for unlimited drives, and Lifetime is $249 with updates for life, according to Unraid’s pricing announcement . Starter and Unleashed include a year of updates, then an optional $36 a year. Unraid’s array lets you mix drive sizes and add one disk at a time, the way Synology’s SHR does, and each drive keeps its own file system, so a failure beyond parity loses only the files on the failed disks. Its Community Apps catalog covers Plex, Jellyfin, Immich, and most other self-hosted software.
 Close modal 
 For hardware, the Minisforum N5 Pro is the most capable box here for either system. It lists at $899 without memory, with a 12-core Ryzen AI 9 HX PRO 370, support for ECC memory up to 96GB, 10GbE plus 5GbE, a PCIe slot, and five bays. ServeTheHome called Minisforum’s own MinisCloud OS a system that still needs work, and Jim’s Garage ran the N5 Pro as a Proxmox host with TrueNAS in a virtual machine, so plan on replacing the stock software. The Minisforum N5 Air keeps the five bays and 10GbE for less: $535 without memory with an 8-core Ryzen 7 255, or $495 with a 6-core Ryzen 5 7640HS. It drops ECC support.
 At the low end, the AOOSTAR WTR Pro 5825U lists at $379 as a four-bay barebone with an 8-core Ryzen 7 5825U and two 2.5GbE ports. It ships with no memory, no system SSD, and no NAS software, so the real starting cost is closer to $450 once you add a memory stick and a small SSD for the operating system. AOOSTAR’s larger WTR MAX adds ECC memory support and 10GbE, and lists at $659 barebone with a Ryzen 7 PRO 8845HS, six SATA bays, five M.2 slots, and two 10GbE SFP+ ports. In early November 2026 it was out of stock at both AOOSTAR’s store and Amazon, so check before you plan around it.
 Replacing Synology’s apps
 Most Synology apps have a free equivalent that runs in Docker on UGOS Pro, QTS, TrueNAS, or Unraid.
 Close modal 
 Synology Photos maps to Immich, a self-hosted Google Photos replacement with face recognition, phone backup, and shared albums. Immich reached its first stable release in October 2025, which ended the project’s long-running warning about breaking changes. UGREEN’s built-in photo app also handles face and object recognition.
 Synology Drive has two common replacements. Nextcloud is a full file-sync suite with calendars and contacts, while Syncthing keeps folders in sync between computers without a server account system.
 Hyper Backup and Snapshot Replication are where the gap is largest. On TrueNAS, ZFS snapshots and replication to a second TrueNAS box keep versioned copies on another machine. On other systems, tools such as Kopia and restic make versioned, encrypted backups to another NAS, a USB drive, or cloud storage, but you set them up yourself. A plain sync to the cloud is not a backup, because a deletion or ransomware encryption on the NAS syncs too.
 Active Backup for Business has no single free equivalent. Macs can back up to a Time Machine share on most NAS systems, and Windows PCs need a separate backup agent. If you back up a dozen office PCs with Active Backup today, that is a strong reason to stay with Synology.
 Surveillance Station users can move to Frigate, an open-source video recorder with object detection. QNAP’s QVR Pro covers simpler camera setups on QNAP hardware.
 Who should stay with Synology
 Synology DiskStation DS925+
 Best for Backups 
 4-Bay 2.5GbE 4GB RAM AMD Ryzen Embedded V1500B 
 List price $700.00 | Full specs 
Check Price on Amazon
 DSM has the most complete backup and maintenance tools of the systems covered here. That matters most when the NAS backs up a few PCs and Macs through Active Backup or Hyper Backup, and when someone else has to look after it with little thought. Third-party hard drives work again for storage pools, so a DS925+ with four WD Red or Seagate IronWolf drives works as a backup appliance. Plan to skip the M.2 cache or buy Synology’s own SSDs, and accept that the box will never hardware-transcode video or go past 2.5GbE.
 If you already own a Synology that still gets updates, there is also no rush. Pair it with a mini PC for Plex, Jellyfin, and Docker, and let the DiskStation keep doing storage and backups. Our guide to setting up a mini PC as a Plex server covers the media side.
 Which Synology alternative to buy
 If you want Buy 
 A four-bay DiskStation replacement with apps UGREEN DXP4800 Plus 
 A two-bay replacement UGREEN DXP2800 
 ZFS on a ready-made box with a PCIe slot QNAP TS-464 with QuTS hero 
 A four-bay box with 5GbE ports and a full NAS system TerraMaster F4-425 Plus (N95 model)

 The cheapest box for TrueNAS or Unraid AOOSTAR WTR Pro 5825U 
 Storage only on a UniFi network UniFi UNAS Pro 
 All-SSD storage for video editing UGREEN DXP480T Plus 
 The best backup software Synology DS925+ 
 If you are not sure a dedicated NAS box is the right shape at all, a small PC with drives attached does much of the same work for less. Our guide to using a mini PC as a NAS covers that route, and the NAS hub lists every model we cover.

results.text:
Best Synology NAS Alternatives in 2026 (What I'd Switch To) 
 Skip to content 
 Post author: Frank Joseph 
 Post published: May 1, 2025 
 Post last modified: July 22, 2026 
 Post category: Synology NAS 
 Reading time: 9 mins read
 Two years ago, “just buy a Synology” was the default answer for anyone who wanted a NAS. Then Synology spent 2025 giving people reasons to look elsewhere: the drive compatibility lock on the 2025 Plus lineup, the move to AMD processors with no hardware transcoding, and a walk-back that came only after the backlash hit sales. I run a Synology alongside a UniFi UNAS Pro 8, a UGREEN NASync, and a TrueNAS box every day, so this isn’t theory. These are the alternatives I’d actually put my data on in 2026, and who each one is right for.
 The short version: the UniFi UNAS Pro is the best prebuilt alternative for pure storage and backups. The UGREEN DXP4800 Plus is the closest thing to a full Synology replacement, apps and Plex transcoding included. TrueNAS is the free answer if you want maximum control on your own hardware, and Unraid is the one to pick if you want to mix drive sizes. TerraMaster and QNAP exist too, and I’ll give you the honest version of both below.
 Disclosure: Some links below are affiliate links, which means that I earn a percentage of each sale at no cost to you. Thank you for your support. 
 Table of Contents 
 show 
 Why People Are Looking for Synology Alternatives in 2026 
 The Two Routes: Prebuilt or DIY 
 UniFi UNAS Pro: The Best Prebuilt Alternative for Pure Storage 
 UGREEN NASync: The Closest Thing to a Full Synology Replacement 
 TrueNAS: The Free Answer for Maximum Control 
 Unraid: The Flexible One for Mixed Drives 
 TerraMaster and QNAP: The Honest Version 
 Synology Alternatives Compared 
 Which Synology Alternative Should You Pick? 
 Conclusion 
 Why People Are Looking for Synology Alternatives in 2026 
 It helps to be clear about what actually happened, because half the “Synology is dead” content out there skips the details. In April 2025, Synology locked the 2025 Plus, Value, and J series to Synology-branded or Synology-certified drives. Third-party drives meant warnings, missing features, and in some cases no storage pool creation at all. The community reaction was exactly what you’d expect, sales reflected it, and in October 2025 Synology reversed course: DSM 7.3 restored third-party 3.5-inch hard drives and 2.5-inch SATA SSDs on the 2025 models. M.2 drives are still restricted, and Synology hasn’t committed to open drive support on future models, so the 2026 lineup remains a question mark.
 On top of that, the current Plus models moved to AMD processors without integrated graphics, which killed hardware transcoding, something I covered in detail in my best NAS for Plex guide . DSM is still the most polished NAS software you can buy, and if your Synology works, there’s no reason to panic-sell it. But the trust hit was real, and if you’re buying new in 2026, the alternatives are better than they’ve ever been.
 The Two Routes: Prebuilt or DIY 
 Every Synology alternative falls into one of two buckets. The first is another prebuilt NAS with its own operating system: UniFi’s UNAS line, UGREEN’s NASync line, TerraMaster, or QNAP. You get hardware and software designed together, a warranty, and the least setup work. The second is running a NAS operating system like TrueNAS or Unraid on hardware you own or build yourself . You trade convenience for control: better hardware for the money, no vendor lock-in, and nobody can change the drive policy on you, because there isn’t one.
 UniFi UNAS Pro: The Best Prebuilt Alternative for Pure Storage 
 The UNAS Pro is the best Synology alternative I’ve used for pure storage. Seven bays and 10G SFP+ networking for $499 is a price Synology simply doesn’t compete with, and the software is the part that sold me. Ubiquiti didn’t try to clone DSM. Snapshots and backups sit right in the drive view, sharing a file externally is a link and a password with no port forwarding, and Time Machine is a checkbox. I ran the original UNAS Pro for close to a year as a daily driver, and it was more reliable than any first-generation product I’ve tested. Today I run the UNAS Pro 8 , the eight-bay version with NVMe caching, as the backup target for a good chunk of my home lab.
 The catch is the whole pitch: UniFi Drive is storage only. No Docker, no apps, no Plex transcoding, and it’s still missing things like iSCSI and encrypted backups. If you need apps, the answer is a cheap mini PC next to it, and I showed exactly how that works in my Docker and Jellyfin on the UNAS Pro guide . If you want to see the whole lineup, including the $199 UNAS 2 and the PoE-powered desktop models, I compared every model in my best UniFi NAS guide .
 UGREEN NASync: The Closest Thing to a Full Synology Replacement 
 If what you want is the complete Synology experience, apps, media serving, photo backup, and all, UGREEN is the alternative that comes closest in 2026. The NASync line launched in 2024, and UGOS Pro has matured a lot since then. It’s still not as refined as DSM, but the gap closes every release, the hardware is consistently a generation ahead of Synology at the same price, and the Intel models handle Plex transcoding that current Synology Plus devices can’t do at all.
 The DXP4800 Plus is the model I’d point most people to, and it’s the unit I’ve tested and reviewed. The DXP2800 is the budget two-bay pick, and the DXP8800 Plus covers big libraries. UGREEN also allows third-party operating systems, so a NASync box can become a TrueNAS or Unraid machine later, which is a nice escape hatch that Synology never gave you. I compared every model in my best UGREEN NAS guide , and if you’re weighing it directly against Synology, I wrote a head-to-head comparison as well.
 TrueNAS: The Free Answer for Maximum Control 
 TrueNAS is a free, open-source NAS operating system built on OpenZFS, and it’s what runs in parallel with my UNAS Pro 8 today. iXsystems has consolidated everything into TrueNAS Community Edition (the old Core and Scale split is effectively over ), apps run on Docker, and the hardware requirements are whatever you want them to be: an old PC, a purpose-built machine , or even a prebuilt NAS you’ve repurposed. Mine runs an Nvidia GPU for AI workloads, which is not a sentence you’ll ever say about a Synology.
 The honest downside is the learning curve. ZFS is the best filesystem you can run at home, but you’ll be learning datasets instead of shared folders, ACLs for permissions, and what ARC actually does to your RAM. None of it is hard once it clicks, and my TrueNAS setup guide walks through all of it, but a Synology refugee should expect a week of feeling lost before it starts making sense.
 Unraid: The Flexible One for Mixed Drives 
 Unraid’s superpower has always been drive flexibility: throw in whatever disks you have, in whatever sizes, and expand one drive at a time, which is something neither ZFS nor Synology’s SHR handles as gracefully. Version 7 added proper ZFS pool support, so you can now run an Unraid array for bulk media and a ZFS pool for the data you care about most, in the same box. The app ecosystem is huge and Docker-based, and the community is one of the best in self-hosting.
 Unlike everything else in the DIY bucket, Unraid is paid software with tiered licenses, and it’s worth knowing that going in. For a media server with a pile of mismatched drives, it’s the best tool for the job and the license pays for itself in drive-reuse alone. For a pure backup box, TrueNAS does it free. I compared the two in my Unraid vs. TrueNAS guide if you’re stuck between them.
 TerraMaster and QNAP: The Honest Version 
 TerraMaster’s hardware is aggressively priced and TOS 6 lays out its backup tools better than most NAS operating systems, but I’ve hit enough bugs in my testing that I can’t recommend it as your primary NAS yet. It improves every year, and I genuinely hope it gets there, but “improving” is not where your data wants to live. QNAP is the more capable of the two: QuTS hero brings real ZFS support to prebuilt hardware, and the spec sheets are strong. The operating system is just a lot, and it’s the one I find least pleasant to actually use. If you’re considering QNAP, try their online demo first, because how QTS feels is the whole decision.
 Synology Alternatives Compared 
 Alternative Type Apps / Docker Plex transcoding Cost Best for 
 UniFi UNAS Pro / Pro 8 Prebuilt, rackmount No (pair a mini PC) No $499 / 7-bay Pure storage + backups 
 UGREEN NASync Prebuilt, desktop Yes Yes (Intel models) $$ hardware only Full Synology replacement 
 TrueNAS CE DIY OS Yes (Docker) Yes (your hardware) Free Control, ZFS, longevity 
 Unraid DIY OS Yes (Docker) Yes (your hardware) Paid license Mixed drives, media servers 
 TerraMaster Prebuilt, desktop Yes Yes (Intel models) $ hardware only Budget, patient users 
 QNAP Prebuilt, desktop Yes Yes (Intel models) $$ hardware only ZFS on prebuilt hardware 
 Which Synology Alternative Should You Pick? 
 You want storage and backups that just work: the UNAS Pro , and the UNAS Pro 8 if you need eight bays. This is what I use for exactly that job.
 You want everything your Synology did, including apps and Plex: the UGREEN DXP4800 Plus .
 You want maximum control and zero vendor decisions in your future: TrueNAS Community Edition on your own hardware. Free, and my DIY NAS build guide covers the hardware side.
 You have a shoebox of mismatched drives and a media server dream: Unraid .
 Your current Synology works fine: keep it. DSM 7.3 restored third-party drive support on the 2025 models, and a working NAS doesn’t need replacing on principle. Just buy the right drives and revisit when it’s actually time.
 Conclusion 
 The real story of 2026 is that “Synology alternative” stopped being a compromise. The UNAS Pro line does storage better per dollar than Synology ever did, UGREEN has nearly closed the software gap while shipping better hardware, and TrueNAS and Unraid turn any box into something more capable than what Synology sells. I know because I run all of them side by side: the UNAS Pro 8 and TrueNAS handle my day-to-day, with a Synology and a UGREEN doing off-site backup duty. Synology walking back the drive lock was the right move, but the lesson stands. Buy the setup that can’t change the rules on you later, and whichever way you go, put good NAS drives in it.

I strongly suggest TrueNAS Scale (Electric Eel update!) or OpenMediaVault8 (OMV). With the rapid shift away from Synology lately, I thought I'd compare it against some of the free and opensource alternatives.

 2026 Verdict The Safety Choice. Best for zero-maintenance. The Best for Plex. Best for growing storage over time. The Security Choice. Best for mission-critical data. The Efficiency Choice. Best for Mini-PCs & old gear. 
 Let's set something straight. Any of the other NAS OS can do what a Synology can do. 
 Is a NAS different than a server? Can they crossover? Hit the link to figure it out once and for all!
 NAS VS SERVER?
 TrueNAS, OMV and Unraid all compete blow for blow vs Synology, or more due to flexibility of the OS and your hardware. They are all definitely cheaper ! Recent UGREEN models have come up in price because they utilize new tech compare to even Synology's new models. For example, the Synology 923+ is using a CPU from 2017 (Ryzen 1600 embedded) but that NAS model was released in 2022.
 Some may say it's a matter of personal opinion on if a different NAS OS can do anything better than Synology, but I argue that once you're released from the limited hardware in a Synology (CPU, memory) you can run any amount of dockers and/or VM's to address any use case you could have. Plus you're not spending a significant sum of funds just on a NAS box, with no hard drives , that you then have to pay even more to upgrade.
 Before we can really compare them, let's dig in a little.
 The "Apple" Mission (Synology): The Set-and-Forget Choice 
 Let’s be upfront: Synology NAS devices aren’t really NAS devices in the purest sense. They're essentially powerful mini-computers built around a dedicated operating system – DiskStation Manager (DSM).
 This is the key differentiator. Synology is to MAC/Apple, what FOSS NAS OS is to the PC! What it is: Synology NAS systems are complete storage and computing solutions. They’re built around a robust, user-friendly operating system (DSM) that handles everything from file sharing and backup to media transcoding, Plex integration, and even basic web server hosting.
 Key Strengths: 
 DSM – The Heart of the System: This is where Synology truly stands out. DSM is incredibly intuitive, packed with features, and offers a huge range of apps and integrations. It’s arguably the best user experience in the NAS market, overall.
 Extensive App Ecosystem: Synology has a massive app store – think Plex, Acronis Cyber Protect, Video Station, Audio Station, and countless others.
 Robust Features: DSM offers advanced features like RAID support (for data redundancy), user permissions, remote access, and even support for Docker containers.
 Scalability: Synology offers a wide range of models, from entry-level to high-performance, allowing you to scale your storage and processing power as your needs grow.
 Community & Support: Synology has a huge and active user community, plus excellent official support.
 Potential Drawbacks: 
 Price: Synology NAS systems are generally more expensive than all other NAS hardware options. Especially more than UGREEN NAS.
 Upgrades possible, but expensive!$! You can upgrade a Synology, depending on model, but for "certified" devices, they charge a premium, just like Apple.
 Complexity: The sheer number of features can be overwhelming for beginners.
 Synology H arddrive Vendor lock in ! If you don't run Synology branded hard drives in their newest devices, you lose support. 
 🤬
 After a ridiculous amount of backlash, Synology relented on this and reverted that change! They are still losing droves of prosumers...
 Synology's storage systems have been transitioning to a more appliance-like business model. Starting with the 25-series, DSM will implement a new HDD compatibility policy in accordance with the published Product Compatibility List. Only listed HDDs are supported for new system installations. This policy is not retroactive and will not affect existing systems and new installations of already released models. Drive migrations from older systems are supported with certain limitations. 
 As of April 2025, the list will consist of Synology drives. Synology intends to constantly update the Product Compatibility List and will introduce a revamped 3rd-party drive validation program. 
 The "Mercenary" Mission (UGREEN): High-Value Hardware 
 UGREEN NAS devices are fundamentally different. They’re essentially pre-built, low-cost NAS-like boxes. They have thier own OS, however the beauty of UGREEN NAS is the ability to install a c ustom NAS OS (often OpenMediaVault or TrueNAS) and are geared towards basic file sharing and storage.
 What it is: UGREEN NAS devices are designed to provide a basic, affordable way to centralize your files and potentially add some network storage capabilities.
 Key Strengths: 
 Price: UGREEN NAS devices are were significantly cheaper than Synology. You can get a functional NAS for a a slightly cheaper cost.
 Can run any NAS OS❗ 
 Ease of Use (Initially): They’re often simpler to set up than Synology, especially for basic file sharing.
 Potential Drawbacks (if running UGREEN OS): 
 Limited Features: They lack the advanced features and robust ecosystem of Synology, yet. Don’t expect Plex transcoding or advanced RAID options out of the box.
 OS Limitations: The underlying operating system is often less polished and offers fewer customization options.
 Community Support: Support is typically limited to the manufacturer’s website and online forums, which may be less active than Synology’s.

 UGREEN NAS DXP6800 Pro 
 The "Tactical" Mission (OpenMediaVault): Lightweight & Efficient 
 If Synology is a pre-built armored vehicle, OpenMediaVault (OMV) is a stripped-down, high-mobility tactical rig. It is built directly on top of Debian 13 Trixie Linux , making it one of the most stable and lightweight NAS operating systems in existence. It’s the go-to choice for those who want a "Digital Fortress" that can run on almost anything—from an old office PC to a Raspberry Pi.
 What it is: OMV is a free, open-source NAS solution that provides a clean web-based interface for managing storage, users, and services. Unlike TrueNAS, which demands significant RAM and specific hardware, OMV is incredibly lean. It doesn't force you into a specific file system; it gives you the keys to the armory and lets you choose your own loadout.
 😉
 This is what Core Lab runs on , and what I chose as my server/NAS OS and have guides written for.
 Key Strengths:
 Ultimate Hardware Flexibility : OMV will run on "toaster" level hardware. It requires as little as 1GB of RAM, making it perfect for repurposing old hardware or building low-power, "silent" NAS nodes.
 Debian Foundation: Because it's just Debian under the hood, any tutorial you find for Linux or Debian usually works on OMV. It is rock-solid and industry-standard.
 Choose Your File System: You aren't locked into ZFS . OMV supports EXT4, XFS, and Btrfs out of the box. Want ZFS? You can add it via the OMV-Extras plugin. You can even make it 'unraid like' and do MergerFS & Snapraid allowing you to mix and match different sized hard drives (similar to Unraid) without the cost!
 Docker-Native (Compose Plugin): With the latest OMV7 and OMV8 releases, the system has moved toward a powerful Docker Compose workflow. You can manage your entire "Arr" stack or media server directly from the web GUI without needing separate tools like Portainer (though you can still use it if you prefer).
 Potential Drawbacks:
 The "Jank" Factor: OMV is a "Lego set." While the UI has improved significantly in 2026, it can still feel a bit "utilitarian" compared to the polished look of Synology or Unraid.
 Update Discipline: Major version upgrades (e.g., OMV7 to OMV8) usually require a bit more "under the hood" attention than a Synology one-click update. It’s a system that rewards those who read the manual.
 Plugin Dependency: To get the "good stuff" (ZFS, Docker, specific backup tools), you must install OMV-Extras. It’s not quite "everything in the box" like its competitors. It's meant to be purpose built.
 Tactical Summary: Choose OMV if you are building on a budget, using a Mini-PC (The Gatehouse), or if you want a system that stays out of your way and lets you manage the OS like a true Linux admin. The "Fortress" Mission (TrueNAS SCALE): Absolute Data Integrity 
 If OMV is a lightweight scout vehicle, TrueNAS SCALE is a main battle tank. It is built on Debian Linux (just like OMV), but it is designed for one thing above all else: absolute data integrity . It uses the ZFS file system natively & by default, which protects your data against "bit rot" and silent corruption using advanced checksums. Their latest release is "Electric Eel" which is more or less, what everyone has been waiting for. This swaps TrueNAS from K8s back to native docker, and you can finally do native ZFS expansion adding a drive at a time!
 What it is: TrueNAS SCALE is the modern, Linux-based successor to the legendary TrueNAS CORE. It combines enterprise-grade storage reliability with "hyper-converged" features like virtual machines and a massive app ecosystem. In late 2024/2025, the "Electric Eel" update replaced its complex backend with Native Docker , making it a massive favorite for homelabbers who previously found it too difficult to use.
 Key Strengths:
 The ZFS Gold Standard: TrueNAS is built around ZFS. Features like Snapshots (allowing you to "roll back" a folder to exactly how it looked 5 minutes ago) and Self-Healing make it the most secure place for your "Digital Fortress" data.
 Native Docker & Compose: No more struggling with "TrueCharts" or Kubernetes. You can now deploy standard Docker containers or paste in a docker-compose.yaml file directly. It is faster, leaner, and finally competes with Unraid on ease of use.
 RAIDZ Expansion (2026 Update): One of the biggest complaints was that you couldn't easily add a single drive to a ZFS array. As of the "Fangtooth" (25.04) release, you can now expand RAIDZ vdevs, making it much more flexible for home users who buy one drive at a time.
 Enterprise Features for Free: You get high-end features like iSCSI (great for booting your PC over the network) and Replication (automatically syncing your NAS to a second offsite unit) without paying a cent.
 Potential Drawbacks:
 RAM Hungry: ZFS loves memory. While OMV can run on 2GB, TrueNAS SCALE really wants 8GB to 16GB of RAM minimum to perform its "self-healing" magic.
 Hardware Picky: It performs best with an HBA (Host Bus Adapter) in IT Mode. Avoid using standard "SATA Expansion cards" or motherboards with "fake RAID" enabled; TrueNAS wants direct, raw access to your drives.
 Complexity: The UI is professional and clean, but the permission settings (ACLs) can be intimidating for beginners. It expects you to understand the difference between a "Pool," a "Vdev," and a "Dataset."
 Tactical Summary: Choose TrueNAS SCALE if your data is irreplaceable (family photos, business docs) and you have modern hardware with at least 16GB of RAM. It is the definitive "Fortress" OS. Performance & Storage Configuration Comparisons 
 Understanding RAID Basics - It's NOT Just About Redundancy!
 Before we get into specific configurations, let’s quickly recap RAID (Redundant Array of Independent Disks). It’s not a magic bullet for data protection, but it can significantly improve performance and/or provide redundancy.RAID 0 (Striping): This is purely for performance. Data is split across all drives. No redundancy – if one drive fails, all your data is lost.RAID 1 (Mirroring): Data is duplicated across all drives. Provides excellent redundancy – if one drive fails, you have a perfect copy. However, you only get the capacity of a single drive.RAID 5 & 6 (Parity): These offer a balance of redundancy and capacity. They use parity information to reconstruct data if a drive fails. RAID 6 can withstand two drive failures.Comparing 6-Bay RAID ConfigurationsLet’s look at how these configurations play out in a 6-bay system:1. RAID 0 (6-Way Striping):Capacity: 6 drives = ~6TB (depending on drive size)Performance: Extremely fast read/write speeds due to parallel data access.Redundancy: None. Catastrophic failure = data loss.Cost: Lowest cost per TB.Ideal For: Users who prioritize speed above all else and are willing to accept the risk of data loss. (e.g., video editing, high-speed backups – with offsite backups!)2. RAID 1 (Mirroring):Capacity: 6 drives = ~6TB (but usable capacity is 3TB)Performance: Read speeds are good, but write speeds are limited by the slowest drive.Redundancy: Excellent – protects against drive failure.Cost: Highest cost per TB at 50% for parity!Ideal For: Users who need reliable data protection and don’t require extreme performance. (e.g., family photo storage, general file sharing)3. RAID 5 & RAID 6 (Parity):Capacity: 6 drives = ~6TB (but usable capacity is 4.5TB - 5TB depending on RAID level)Performance: Read speeds are good, but write speeds are slower than RAID 0 due to parity calculations.Redundancy: RAID 5 can withstand one drive failure. RAID 6 can withstand two drive failures.Cost: Moderate cost per TB.Ideal For: A good balance of redundancy and capacity for most users. RAID 6 is generally recommended for critical data.
 Storage Hybrid RAID (SHR)
 Overview: Developed by Synology, SHR is a software RAID solution that dynamically adapts to the number of drives in the array. It intelligently stripes data across drives to maximize capacity while maintaining performance. It’s not a traditional RAID level; it’s a method of managing drives.Pros:Efficient Capacity Utilization: Shrines drives of different sizes together, using the largest drives for performance and the smaller ones for capacity.Good Performance: Offers performance close to RAID 5/6 while using fewer drives.Automatic Drive Management: Handles drive failures and rebuilds automatically.Cons:Synology Ecosystem: Primarily designed for Synology NAS devices.Rebuild Times: Can have longer rebuild times compared to traditional RAID 5/6, especially with large drives.Typical Use Cases: Ideal for users who want a balance of capacity, performance, and redundancy, particularly with Synology NAS systems.
 ZFS with RAID-Z (RAID-Z1 & RAID-Z2)
 Overview: ZFS is a powerful, advanced file system known for its data integrity features, snapshots, and scalability. RAID-Z (formerly RAID-5) is ZFS's native RAID implementation.RAID-Z1: Similar to RAID 5 – tolerates one drive failure.RAID-Z2: Tolerates two drive failures – a significant advantage over RAID 5/6. The more drives you scale up with, the more storage efficiency you gain.Pros:Data Integrity: ZFS’s checksumming and self-healing capabilities provide exceptional data protection.Snapshots & Cloning: Excellent support for snapshots and clones.Scalability: Handles huge storage arrays effectively.Advanced Caching: ZFS utilizes RAM as a cache automatically, greatly boosting performance.Cons:Resource Intensive: Requires more CPU and RAM than traditional RAID.Complexity: Can be more complex to configure and manage.Hardware Compatibility: Requires a hardware controller for optimal performance.Typical Use Cases: Critical data storage, virtual machine storage, environments requiring high data integrity.
 Unraid
 Overview: Unraid is a software-based NAS operating system that utilizes a unique "bucket" system. It's designed for ease of use, flexibility, and cost-effectiveness. Unlike traditional RAID, it doesn't stripe data across drives. Instead, it creates individual "buckets" on each drive, allowing for expansion and flexible storage allocation.Pros:Ease of Use: Very user-friendly interface, simple drive expansion.Flexibility: Each drive is independent, allowing for variable drive sizes.Cost-Effective: Lower initial hardware cost, especially with smaller drives.Snapshots: Excellent snapshot functionality.Cons:Performance Limitations: Performance can be limited by the CPU and RAM, particularly with large numbers of drives.No True RAID: Doesn't offer the redundancy benefits of traditional RAID unless an additional parity disk is added.Limited Advanced Features: Lacks some of the advanced features of ZFS.Typical Use Cases: Home media servers, small business file sharing, users prioritizing ease of use and flexibility.
 Performance Comparison Tables (Expanded) 
 RAID Level/Method Read Speed Write Speed IOPS Data Integrity Capacity Efficiency 
 RAID 0 Fastest Fastest Highest None Poor 
 RAID 1 Good Slow Moderate Excellent Excellent

 Unraid Moderate Moderate Moderate Limited Excellent 
 ZFS vs UNRAID: 
 Data Integrity: ZFS (RAID-Z1/2) and traditional RAID 1 offer superior data integrity compared to Unraid. Unraid relies primarily on backups.
 Capacity Efficiency: Unraid excels in capacity efficiency, allowing for variable drive sizes and easy expansion. ZFS and traditional RAID are less flexible.
 Complexity: Unraid is the easiest to set up and manage. ZFS can be the most complex.
 ZFS vs Traditional RAID & SHR: 
 Data Integrity: ZFS (RAID-Z1/2) is significantly better at protecting against data corruption than traditional RAID. Traditional RAID relies on parity, which can be less reliable.
 Capacity Efficiency: SHR is the most efficient in terms of utilizing drive sizes. ZFS is less efficient, but still better than traditional RAID.
 Complexity: ZFS is the most complex to manage, requiring a deeper understanding of the file system. SHR is relatively easy to use within the Synology ecosystem.
 Hardware Controller: ZFS strongly benefits from a hardware RAID controller for optimal performance. While it can run on software controllers, performance will be limited.
 Which is Right for You? 
 Hardware NAS? 
 Choose Synology if: You need a robust, feature-rich NAS for a wide range of tasks, including media server hosting, backup, virtualization, and advanced data management. You’re willing to invest more money and time to learn the system.
 Choose UGREEN if: You’re on a tight budget and just need a basic NAS for simple file sharing and storage. You’re comfortable with a more limited system and don’t require advanced features.
 Software NAS (Custom NAS)? 
 Choose OMV7, TrueNAS or Unraid on a Custom NAS if : You want ultimate flexibility, avoid vendor lock-in, want to enjoy affordable upgrades, virtualization & advanced use cases on a system that you build yourself. The potential is massive.
 Core Lab is running on a custom purpose built-"NAS". See here. 
 The Final Mission Briefing: Which Path Will You Take?
 Choosing your NAS OS is like choosing your primary base of operations. The hardware is the walls, but the OS is the intelligence agency running inside. To make your final choice, you must identify your primary mission profile. 
 🛑 Profile 1: The "Zero-Dark-Thirty" (Synology)
 The Mission: You need a system that works 24/7 with zero intervention. You want your family's photos backed up, your files synced, and a polished mobile app for every member of the "unit."
 Choose this if: You value your time more than your hardware freedom. You don't want to learn Linux; you want to "deploy and enjoy."
 The Gear: [Synology DS923+ or DS1522+]
 🛠️ Profile 2: The "Scrap-Metal Tech" (OpenMediaVault)
 The Mission: You’re repurposing an old office PC or a low-power Mini-PC (The Gatehouse). You want a lean, mean machine that doesn't waste a single CPU cycle on "bloatware."
 Choose this if: You’re on a budget, building a "hidden" edge node, or want a pure Debian experience where you control every single Docker container via YAML.
 The Gear: [Intel N150 Mini-PC / Used Dell Optiplex]
 The Core Labs choice! 
 🎬 Profile 3: The "Digital Hoarder" (Unraid)
 The Mission: You have a collection of 10TB, 14TB, and 18TB drives you’ve "shucked" over the years. You want the easiest way to run Plex, download your media, and add more storage whenever a sale hits.
 Choose this if: Your main goal is a media server and you want the most flexible "Mix-and-Match" drive array on the planet.
 The Gear: [Custom Build in a Jonsbo N3 or Fractal Node 804]
 🛡️ Profile 4: The "Fortress Commander" (TrueNAS SCALE)
 The Mission: You are storing irreplaceable data (business records, a decade of RAW photography). You want the "Gold Standard" of data protection (ZFS) and you have the RAM to back it up.
 Choose this if: Data integrity is your #1 priority and you want to use the same file system that enterprise data centers trust. (Bonus: The 2026 "Electric Eel" update makes this easier than ever for Docker users).
 The Gear: [Enterprise-grade hardware / 32GB+ ECC RAM]
 Final Tactical Tip: "RAID is Not a Backup"
 No matter which OS you choose, remember the 3-2-1 Rule :
 3 copies of your data.
 2 different media types (NAS + External Drive).
 1 copy offsite (Cloud or a "Buddy Backup" at a friend's house).
 Core Lab Simple Backup Guide here.
 Your Digital Fortress is only as strong as your weakest link. Secure your data, commander. 
 ❓ Frequently Asked Questions (FAQ)
 What is the best NAS OS for a beginner?
 Synology's DSM is the best fit if you want a "set-and-forget" experience with minimal tinkering — it trades some flexibility and cost-efficiency for a polished, appliance-like interface and rock-solid reliability.
 Which NAS OS is best for absolute data integrity?
 TrueNAS SCALE, built on ZFS, is the strongest choice for data integrity. ZFS checksums every block of data and can detect and self-heal silent corruption ("bit rot"), which matters most if you're storing irreplaceable files long-term.
 Can I mix different sized hard drives in my NAS?
 It depends on the OS. Unraid is specifically built around mixing and matching drive sizes without needing them to match, which is a major advantage if you're building your array gradually from whatever drives you already own. ZFS-based systems (TrueNAS, OMV with ZFS) generally want matched drives per pool for best results.
 Is OpenMediaVault a good choice for older or lower-power hardware?
 Yes — OMV is deliberately lightweight and efficient, making it a strong fit for repurposed or lower-spec hardware where a heavier platform would feel sluggish, while still supporting ZFS and Docker for a capable modern NAS.
 Do I still need backups if my NAS uses RAID or ZFS?
 Yes — RAID is not a backup. It protects against a drive failure, not against accidental deletion, ransomware, or the whole unit being destroyed. Follow the 3-2-1 rule: 3 copies of your data, on 2 different media types, with 1 copy stored offsite.

 A NAS can be a simple private cloud, a multi-drive backup target, a Plex server, or a fast shared workspace. The right model depends less on the brand name than on three questions: how much storage you need, whether you need drive-failure protection, and how fast your network and client devices are.
 For most buyers, the Synology BeeStation is the easiest single-drive option, while the QNAP TS-233 is the better starting point for a conventional two-bay NAS. Power users should look at the faster ASUSTOR, Synology, or TerraMaster models below. We have also included specialist choices for SSD storage and local AI features.

 Synology BeeStation: Best single-drive NAS for most people
 The Synology BeeStation is the least intimidating way to get network storage. It arrives with a fixed 4TB internal drive, so there is no drive-shopping exercise, RAID configuration, or disk installation before you can start storing files. It supports remote access and has both USB-A and USB-C ports for importing or copying data.
 The trade-off is fundamental: this is a single-drive product, not a conventional multi-bay Synology DiskStation. There is no internal RAID, so a failed drive can make the stored data unavailable. It also does not offer Synology’s usual DSM application catalog. Treat it as a convenient private cloud and backup destination, not as a server platform for a large collection of services.
 Popular on Amazon
 Synology BeeStation 4TB Personal Cloud Storage Device (BST151-4T) | Automatic Photo & Video Backup, No Subscription Required 
 Set up a personal cloud in minutes and get right into data managing works
 Bring files from computers, tablets, phones, external drives, and supported cloud accounts into one place for remote access and management. Back up photos from your phone and iCloud Photos, then use local AI to identify people or subjects.
 Sync files: Edit files on your desktop while keeping changes synced across your computers.
 Local AI: Uses an onboard GPU to run photo recognition, making it easy to search and sort images by subject or location without touching the public cloud.
 Backup and recovery: Automated snapshots allow you to go back in time and recover previous versions of your files, protecting against malware and accidental changes.
 $399.99 
 Buy on Amazon 
 Check the exact model before buying. The original BST150-4T uses a Realtek RTD1619B processor and 1GB of RAM, while BeeStation Plus models such as the BST170 series use an Intel Celeron J4125 and 4GB of memory. The 8TB BST170-8T is a different hardware configuration from the original 4TB model.
 QNAP TS-233: Best two-bay NAS for most people
 The QNAP TS-233 is the sensible step up from a single-drive box. Its two hot-swappable bays accept 3.5-inch hard drives or 2.5-inch SATA SSDs, allowing you to configure RAID 1 and keep a mirrored copy of data on both drives. It is a good fit for home documents, photos, laptop backups, and basic media-serving duties.
 Its hardware is deliberately modest: a quad-core ARM Cortex-A55 processor running at 2GHz and 2GB of onboard, non-expandable RAM. Networking is limited to one 1GbE port. That is sufficient for ordinary household file sharing, but it is not the model to choose for heavy virtualization, large container workloads, or a fast editing workstation.
 The TS-233 has two USB 2.0 ports and one USB 3.2 Gen 1 port. Those are useful for external drives and peripherals, but they do not provide a substitute for a multi-gigabit network connection.
 ASUSTOR Drivestor 2 Gen2 AS1202T: Best budget NAS
 The ASUSTOR Drivestor 2 Gen2 AS1202T offers more network bandwidth than many entry-level two-bay NAS devices. Its 2.5GbE port can help when the NAS, switch, and client computer all support 2.5GbE, and it provides three USB Type-A ports rated at 5Gbps.
 ASUSTOR’s ADM operating system supports more than 150 applications, giving this enclosure broader software potential than a basic file server. Its two 3.5-inch bays can also be configured for redundancy or capacity, depending on your priorities.
 The key omission is HDMI. If you want to connect the NAS directly to a television or monitor, this is the wrong pick. Also remember that 2.5GbE only matters when the rest of the network can carry it; connected to a standard gigabit switch, it will operate within that slower limit.
 ASUSTOR Lockerstor 2 Gen2+ AS6702T v2: Best two-bay NAS for power users
 The AS6702T v2 puts unusually serious connectivity and expansion into a two-bay chassis. It has dual 5GbE ports, 4GB of DDR4-2933 memory, two USB ports rated at 10Gbps, and four M.2 NVMe slots.
 The M.2 slots are particularly useful because they can be used for SSD caching, storage, or a combination of both. That flexibility is not universal: on some NAS models, M.2 slots are cache-only. The two SATA bays still provide the bulk storage, while NVMe drives can add a fast pool or accelerate selected workloads.
 It uses a quad-core Intel Celeron N5105 and supports features such as link aggregation and 4K transcoding. Neither feature guarantees a particular result. Transcoding depends on the codec, container, audio track, subtitles, client, and software. Link aggregation also does not make one ordinary file transfer automatically run at twice the speed.
 ASUSTOR Lockerstor 4 Gen 3 AS6804T: Best four-bay NAS for power users
 The AS6804T is built for demanding networks and large storage pools. It combines four SATA bays with two 10GbE ports, two 5GbE ports, four PCIe 4.0 M.2 slots, two USB4 ports, and three USB 3.2 Gen 2 Type-A ports.
 Its 16GB of ECC DDR5-4800 memory is expandable to 64GB, making it a much stronger candidate for containers, multiple services, and heavier multitasking than entry-level NAS hardware. The USB4 ports can work with Thunderbolt 3 and Thunderbolt 4 devices, which may be useful for fast direct-attached workflows.
 Do not interpret the port count as a promise of 10Gbps transfers in every setup. You need compatible switches, cabling, and client hardware, and hard drives or a particular RAID layout may become the bottleneck. Manufacturer throughput figures are laboratory results under optimized conditions.
 Also popular on Amazon

 $159.99

 Synology DiskStation DS1525+: Best five-bay NAS for power users
 The Synology DS1525+ is the most expandable general-purpose choice in this group. It has five bays for 3.5-inch SATA hard drives or 2.5-inch SATA SSDs, two 2.5GbE ports, two M.2 2280 slots, and two expansion-unit ports. An optional E10G22-T1-Mini module adds 10GbE networking.
 Supported storage layouts include Synology Hybrid RAID (SHR), Basic, JBOD, RAID 0, RAID 1, RAID 5, RAID 6, and RAID 10. Five bays give you room to start with fewer drives and add capacity later, although changing a storage layout still requires planning, backups, and time for rebuilding.
 The M.2 slots are for SSD cache and are not hot-swappable. Synology says the system can reach up to 360TB of raw capacity with two DX525 expansion units and 24TB drives. That is raw installed capacity, not the usable space after RAID, filesystem overhead, and reserved system capacity.
 Drive compatibility deserves attention. Synology’s 2025 Plus-series policy introduced stricter requirements around Synology drives and third-party drives certified to Synology specifications. DSM 7.3 and later provide greater flexibility for third-party HDDs and 2.5-inch SATA SSDs in 2025 Plus models, but you should still check the model-specific compatibility list. Drives outside the list may receive limited support.
 LatticeWork Amber X: Best single-SSD NAS
 The LatticeWork Amber X is a compact alternative to a traditional disk-based NAS. It includes a 512GB internal SSD, wired and wireless networking, HDMI output, remote access, and a USB 3.1 port for external storage.
 It is a useful fit for a small personal file library, mobile-photo workflow, or living-room media device. AI facial recognition is included among its features, and HDMI makes it more flexible as a direct media appliance than most NAS products.
 The internal SSD is not a multi-drive RAID array. If the data matters, attach external storage or maintain another backup. Its capacity also makes it unsuitable as the sole home for a large video archive.
 TerraMaster F8 SSD Plus: Best multi-SSD NAS
 The TerraMaster F8 SSD Plus is an eight-bay NVMe NAS, not an eight-bay enclosure for 3.5-inch hard drives. You supply the M.2 SSDs, then configure them using modes including TRAID, TRAID+, Basic, JBOD, RAID 0, RAID 1, RAID 5, RAID 6, or RAID 10.
 With 10GbE, HDMI, USB connectivity, and TerraMaster’s TOS 6 operating system, it is aimed at users who want high-throughput solid-state storage for projects, media, or multiple users. Eight NVMe drives can deliver far more parallel storage performance than a small hard-drive NAS, but the SSD budget can quickly exceed the cost of the enclosure.
 Any price quoted for this model must be checked carefully. The commonly cited $800 figure refers to the enclosure without SSDs and is a dated purchase-price reference. Your actual system cost depends on eight compatible NVMe drives, cooling, and the network hardware needed to use 10GbE.
 Zettlab D4 AI NAS: Best AI-augmented NAS
 The Zettlab D4 AI NAS combines four SATA bays with local AI features. It has a 2.5GbE port, a 1GbE port, HDMI, SD and TF card readers, 16GB of LPDDR4x memory, one M.2 slot, and an RK3588 processor with a 6-TOPS neural-processing unit.
 Its software features include AI Search, Knowledge QA, Photo Album, Auto Transcription, and AI Clip. Zettlab says the AI processing runs locally, which can be attractive for users who want photo organization and search without sending their library to a cloud service.
 The D4 supports JBOD, Basic, RAID 0, RAID 1, RAID 5, RAID 6, and RAID 10. Its advertised maximum of 100TB is a manufacturer calculation based on four 24TB drives and a 4TB M.2 drive; it is not the guaranteed usable capacity of a RAID 5 setup.
 Also popular on Amazon
 Sale 
 Synology DS223 Home & Office Backup Hub - Centralize Files, Protect Data & Monitor Property (2-Bay Diskless NAS) 
 One Place for All Your Data - Consolidate scattered files from multiple computers, phones and external drives into one accessible hub with 100% ownership
 Professional File Collaboration - Share projects with clients, sync documents across teams and maintain version control without Dropbox fees
 Automated Backup Protection - Set-and-forget backups for Macs, PCs and mobile devices to multiple destinations including cloud and external drives
 DIY Surveillance System - Transform IP cameras into a professional monitoring solution with motion alerts, recording schedules and remote viewing
 2-Year Warranty - Reliable hardware backed by Synology's expert customer support team and ongoing software updates
 $285.99 
 Buy on Amazon 
 Independent reader support Your contribution helps us test, update, and keep practical guides available for everyone. Support on Ko-Fi How to choose a NAS
 1. Decide whether you need redundancy
 A single-drive NAS is convenient, but it has no internal protection from drive failure. In a two-bay system, RAID 1 mirrors the data and sacrifices half of the raw capacity. RAID 5 needs at least three drives and tolerates one failure; RAID 6 needs at least four and tolerates two; RAID 10 needs at least four and combines mirroring with striping.
 RAID is not a backup. It will not save files deleted by mistake, data encrypted by malware, or a NAS destroyed by theft, fire, flooding, or a failed power supply. Keep a separate backup, preferably one that is disconnected or otherwise protected from ransomware.
 2. Match the network to the workload
 Network link 
 Best fit 
 Common limitation 
 1GbE 
 Documents, backups, music, ordinary home streaming 
 About 125MB per second of theoretical link bandwidth before overhead 
 2.5GbE 
 Large photo libraries, faster backups, several users 
 Requires a 2.5GbE client or switch path to matter 
 5GbE or 10GbE 
 Video work, large project files, SSD arrays, busy offices 
 Storage media, cabling, switches, and the client can bottleneck transfers 
 A faster Ethernet port does not automatically make hard drives faster. File size, RAID level, protocol overhead, simultaneous users, and the speed of the client system all affect real-world throughput.
 3. Check what the M.2 slots actually do
 M.2 does not always mean “add an NVMe storage pool.” The DS1525+ specifies its M.2 slots for cache, while the AS6702T v2 and AS6804T can use M.2 drives for caching, storage, or both. Read the model’s storage documentation before buying SSDs for a role the NAS does not support.
 4. Budget for drives and backups
 Most NAS enclosures are sold without drives. Calculate usable capacity after RAID rather than adding the printed capacities together. Also include the cost of a second backup destination, UPS protection if the NAS is important, and replacement drives with an approved compatibility status.
 How we test NAS devices
 NAS recommendations are based on hands-on testing in PC Labs, including file-transfer performance and the range and quality of available NAS applications. Specifications matter, but they are not the whole result: a 10GbE port is less useful when a product’s software is awkward, and a simple 1GbE NAS may be the better purchase for a household that values easy setup over maximum throughput.
 FAQ
 Is a NAS better than an external hard drive?
 A NAS is better when several devices need shared access, remote access, automated backups, or services such as media libraries. An external drive is cheaper and simpler for a single computer. A NAS should not replace an external or off-site backup.
 What is the best NAS for a beginner?
 The Synology BeeStation is the easiest option if you want a preconfigured 4TB private-cloud device and can accept the lack of RAID. Choose the QNAP TS-233 instead if you want a conventional two-bay NAS with mirrored RAID 1 and more room to expand.
 Does RAID protect my files?
 RAID protects availability when a supported drive fails, depending on the RAID level. It does not protect against accidental deletion, corruption, malware, theft, fire, or a failed NAS. Maintain a separate backup.
 Do I need 10GbE for a home NAS?
 Usually not. 1GbE is adequate for ordinary documents, backups, and media streaming, while 2.5GbE is a practical upgrade for large transfers. 10GbE becomes worthwhile with SSD storage, video-editing workloads, or multiple active users—and only when the switch and client devices support it.
 The Bottom Line
 The Synology BeeStation is the easiest single-drive choice, but its fixed disk and lack of RAID make a second backup essential. For a conventional home NAS, the QNAP TS-233 is the more flexible starting point. The ASUSTOR AS1202T is a strong budget alternative with 2.5GbE, while the AS6702T v2, AS6804T, and Synology DS1525+ make more sense when you need faster networking, more bays, or heavier workloads.
 Choose the TerraMaster F8 SSD Plus for an all-NVMe build and the Zettlab D4 when local AI organization is central to your plans. Whichever model you buy, plan the storage layout, verify drive compatibility, and keep a backup that is not dependent on the NAS itself.

Best Synology Alternatives: UGREEN vs QNAP vs UniFi UNAS vs DIY | ComputingForGeeks
