 Synology removed its third-party hard drive block in DSM 7.3, so drive choice is no longer the main reason to look for the best Synology alternative. The reasons that remain are hardware and software: a DS925+ at about $770 still ships 4 GB of RAM, two 2.5GbE ports and a Ryzen V1500B with no integrated GPU, and an unlisted M.2 NVMe drive still cannot form a storage pool on any 2025 Synology model.
 Original content from computingforgeeks.com - post 173077 
 This guide covers the four appliance brands that replace a DiskStation (UGREEN, QNAP, TerraMaster and UniFi UNAS) plus a DIY TrueNAS or Unraid build. It maps each major DSM app to its equivalent on every platform, and it closes with a copy plan that moves a full Synology volume without the proprietary Hyper Backup archive format.
 Compared October 2026 against DSM 7.4.1. 
 Best Synology alternatives: quick picks
 Award Pick Price (check live) Why it wins 
 Best overall UGREEN DXP4800 Plus about $657 Replaces a DS925+ for about $110 less, with 8 GB DDR5, 10GbE and Quick Sync 
 Best value QNAP TS-464-8G about $509 Closest app set to DSM, including free bare-metal PC backup and an 8-channel NVR 
 Best 2-bay UGREEN DXP2800 about $390 8 GB RAM and two M.2 slots that can hold a storage pool, against 2 GB and no M.2 on the DS225+ 
 Best SHR replacement TerraMaster F4-425 Pro about $700 (about $595 direct) TRAID mixes drive sizes the way SHR does; 8-core N305 and two 5GbE ports 
 Best backup target UniFi UNAS Pro 4 about $549 at store.ui.com, surcharge included Two 10G SFP+ ports, Time Machine and rsync pull from a DiskStation, for less than a DS425+ 
 Best DIY Jonsbo N3 case about $150 (case only) Eight 3.5-inch bays for TrueNAS or Unraid, with no vendor OS between you and the disks 
 What still pushes owners off Synology in 2026
 The October 2025 reversal is narrower than most coverage suggests. The Synology drive compatibility policy page splits the rules by product line, and the M.2 rule did not change for any of them. The policy covers models launched from 2025 onward; older units such as the DS923+ were never affected.
 2025+ model line, DSM 7.3 and later Unlisted HDD Unlisted 2.5-inch SATA SSD Unlisted M.2 NVMe 
 DS Plus and desktop FS (DS225+, DS425+, DS925+, DS1825+) New pool allowed New pool and cache allowed Migration only, no new pool or cache 
 Value and J series New pool allowed Allowed Not applicable (no M.2 row) 
 RS Plus rackmounts Migration only Allowed, marked unverified Migration only 
 XS, XS+, rackmount FS, SA, HD, UC Migration only Migration only Migration only 
 Five problems remain after the reversal, and each one is measurable:
 NVMe pricing. The Synology SNV5420-400G lists at about $587 on Amazon against about $237 for a 1 TB Samsung 990 EVO Plus. That is 2.5x the price for 40% of the capacity, or $1.47 per GB against $0.24.
 A new feature lock. DSM 7.4 requires Synology hard drives for post-processing deduplication and compression, and the three Synology HAT3310 12 TB and 16 TB Amazon listings checked for this guide are out of stock.
 Media processing moved off the box. DSM 7.2.2 removed Video Station and handed HEVC, H.264 and VC-1 processing to client devices, and DSM 7.3 kept that change. The 2025 J4125 models also ship without the Intel i915 driver, so Plex hardware transcoding needs a community workaround over SSH, while the R1600 and V1500B models have no GPU at all.
 RAM. The DS225+ and DS425+ ship 2 GB onboard plus one empty slot, 6 GB maximum; UGREEN and QNAP ship 8 GB in the same price band.
 End of updates. DSM 7.4 is the last major version for the DS918+, DS218+, DS718+, DS1019+, DS1618+, DS1819+ and DS2419+, which puts a deadline on most 2016 to 2019 Plus, Value and J models still in service.
 None of this makes DSM a bad operating system. Active Backup for Business, Synology Photos and Hyper Backup remain the most complete bundle on any appliance, and the app map further down shows where every alternative falls short of them.
 How the picks were chosen
 Every number in this guide comes from a manufacturer spec page or datasheet, cross-checked against a live retailer listing and one independent review. Amazon prices, sellers and stock were read through the Amazon Creators API on October 5, 2026, and each pick is sold by the manufacturer or by Amazon itself. Idle power figures come from the cited reviews, because UGREEN lists an identical 42.36 W figure for four different models (three 4-bay, one 2-bay). None of these units was benchmarked on the test bench for this guide; the measured transcode and drive numbers live in the linked articles.
 Excluded: the ARM-based UGREEN DH2300 (no Docker) and DH4300 Plus (no virtual machines), the QNAP TS-462A (costs more than the TS-464 with one 2.5GbE port and no PCIe slot), the TerraMaster N95 variants (the manufacturer spec text contradicts itself on RAM type and clock), the Asustor AS5404T (only available from a third-party seller), and the TrueNAS Mini X+ (sold direct for $2,160 diskless, more than three times the price of a DXP4800 Plus).
 Synology alternatives compared
 The two Synology rows are the baseline. Hardware transcoding means an iGPU that Plex or Jellyfin can use without a workaround.
 Model Price CPU and HW transcode RAM shipped / max Bays + M.2 pool Network Warranty 
 Synology DS925+ about $770 Ryzen V1500B, no iGPU 4 GB ECC / 32 GB 4 + 2 (Synology NVMe only) 2x 2.5GbE 3 years 
 Synology DS425+ about $598 Celeron J4125, i915 removed 2 GB / 6 GB 4 + 2 (Synology NVMe only) 1GbE + 2.5GbE 3 years 
 UGREEN DXP4800 Plus about $657 Pentium Gold 8505, Quick Sync 8 GB DDR5 / 64 GB 4 + 2 Gen4, any brand 10GbE + 2.5GbE 2 years 
 QNAP TS-464-8G about $509 Celeron N5095, Quick Sync 8 GB DDR4 / 16 GB 4 + 2 Gen3 x1 2x 2.5GbE, PCIe Gen3 x2 slot 3 years 
 UGREEN DXP2800 about $390 N100, Quick Sync 8 GB DDR5 / 16 GB 2 + 2 1x 2.5GbE 2 years 
 TerraMaster F4-425 Pro about $700 Core i3-N305, Quick Sync 8 GB DDR5 / 32 GB 4 + 3 Gen3 x1 2x 5GbE 2 years 
 UniFi UNAS Pro 4 about $549 4x Cortex-A57 ARM, none 8 GB, not upgradeable 4 + 2 (cache only) 2x 10G SFP+ + 1GbE 2 years direct 
 DIY: Jonsbo N3 about $150 + board Your choice Your choice 8 + board M.2 Board dependent Per part 
 1. UGREEN DXP4800 Plus: best overall Synology replacement
 UGREEN NASync DXP4800 Plus: Pentium Gold 8505, 8 GB DDR5, 10GbE plus 2.5GbE. Image: UGREEN. 
 The DXP4800 Plus is the direct answer to a DS925+: four bays, two M.2 slots and a newer Intel CPU, for about $110 less on Amazon at the time of writing. It suits a DS920+ or DS918+ owner who runs Docker containers, Plex or Jellyfin, and a few shares, and who wants 10GbE without an add-in card.
 CPU: Pentium Gold 8505, 5 cores and 6 threads, with UHD Graphics (48 EU) and Quick Sync for hardware transcoding.
 Memory: 8 GB DDR5 in two SODIMM slots, 64 GB maximum. The UGREEN “ODECC” label refers to the on-die error correction built into DDR5, not system ECC.
 Storage: four SATA bays, two PCIe 4.0 M.2 slots that accept any brand as cache or as a separate pool, and a 128 GB boot SSD that keeps UGOS Pro off the data drives.
 Network: one 10GbE port and one 2.5GbE port. KitGuru measured 24.25 W idle on 2.5GbE and 30.45 W on 10GbE with four WD Red drives installed.
 Warranty: 2 years, one year shorter than the Synology term of 3.
 The catch: it is the wrong box for anyone who depends on Active Backup for Business or Surveillance Station. UGREEN documents file-level PC backup but no bare-metal image backup, and the UGOS Pro feature list names no NVR app. Pool portability is the second catch: an investigation by a UGREEN customer found that UGOS Btrfs and ext4 pools set on-disk feature flags that stock Linux refuses to mount, while Synology documents how to read an SHR volume on Ubuntu. The BIOS is open, so TrueNAS or Unraid can replace UGOS Pro on the same hardware, and the TrueNAS and Unraid guide for the UGREEN Ultra models covers the BIOS steps on the same family.
 Check price on Amazon 
 2. QNAP TS-464-8G: best value and the closest app set to DSM
 QNAP TS-464-8G: Celeron N5095, 8 GB DDR4, 2x 2.5GbE, PCIe Gen3 x2 slot. Image: QNAP. 
 QTS is the only alternative OS that matches DSM app for app. HDP PC Agent does free full-system and bare-metal PC backup, HDP for PC/VM backs up VMware and Hyper-V without licences, HBS 3 replaces Hyper Backup, Qsync replaces Synology Drive, and QVR Pro includes 8 camera channels free (playing back recordings older than 14 days in QVR Pro Client needs the paid Unlimited Playback licence). At about $509 sold by Amazon.com, it is also about $90 cheaper than a DS425+ and ships four times its RAM.
 CPU: Celeron N5095, 4 cores, with UHD Graphics for hardware transcoding.
 Memory: 8 GB DDR4 in two slots, 16 GB maximum. QuTS hero (ZFS) needs 8 GB, so the 8G model can run it.
 Storage: four bays and two M.2 2280 slots at PCIe Gen3 x1, usable as cache or storage.
 Expansion: a PCIe Gen3 x2 slot, the only one among the 4-bay picks here, which takes a 10GbE card or an M.2 adapter.
 Network and power: two 2.5GbE ports; QNAP rates it at 21.6 W with disks in standby and 40.5 W in operation. Warranty is 3 years.
 Where it falls short: headroom. The N5095 platform dates from 2021, the RAM ceiling is 16 GB, and each M.2 slot runs at about 1 GB/s. The QNAP security record also needs to be part of the decision: Qlocker in April 2021 and DeadBolt in January 2022 hit internet-exposed QTS boxes, and the TS-453E was compromised several times at Pwn2Own Ireland 2025 (the DS925+ was rooted twice at the same event). Keep QTS off the public internet, reach it through a VPN, and apply QSA advisories as they ship.
 Check price on Amazon 
 3. UGREEN DXP2800: best 2-bay replacement for a DS225+
 UGREEN NASync DXP2800: Intel N100, 8 GB DDR5, two M.2 slots, 2.5GbE. Image: UGREEN. 
 The DS225+ costs about $365 and ships 2 GB of RAM with no M.2 slot. The DXP2800 costs about $25 more and ships 8 GB DDR5 plus two M.2 slots that can hold an SSD pool for Docker volumes and app data. It fits a 2-bay home server: photo backup, a Jellyfin library and a handful of containers.
 CPU: Intel N100, 4 cores, with Quick Sync. Ocinside measured about 7 W idle and 34.7 W at maximum load.
 Memory: 8 GB DDR5, 16 GB maximum.
 Storage: two bays, two M.2 slots (cache or pool), and a 32 GB eMMC boot device rather than a boot SSD.
 Network: a single 2.5GbE port. Warranty is 2 years.
 Look elsewhere if the NAS feeds a 10GbE desktop. The DXP2800 GT adds a 10GbE port for about $460, but it swaps the N100 for an AMD Ryzen R2514, which has no Quick Sync and no AV1 decode, so Plex transcoding is weaker on it. The same trade applies one size up, where the DXP4800 GT gives two 10GbE ports for about $560.
 Check price on Amazon 
 4. TerraMaster F4-425 Pro: best SHR replacement for mixed drive sizes
 TerraMaster F4-425 Pro: Core i3-N305, 8 GB DDR5, three M.2 slots, 2x 5GbE. Image: TerraMaster. 
 SHR is the feature Synology owners miss first. It lets a pool grow one larger drive at a time while still using the full capacity of mixed sizes. Among the appliance brands here, only TRAID in TerraMaster TOS 7 offers the same model; UGOS Pro, QTS and UniFi Drive all use fixed RAID levels. The F4-425 Pro pairs TRAID with the strongest CPU in this price class.
 CPU: Core i3-N305, 8 cores, with UHD Graphics (32 EU) and Quick Sync.
 Memory: 8 GB DDR5 in a single slot. TerraMaster lists 32 GB, while Intel ARK lists 16 GB as the official maximum for the N305.
 Storage: four bays and three M.2 2280 slots at PCIe 3.0 x1, which can form their own RAID 5 SSD pool.
 Network: two 5GbE ports, which reach roughly half of 10GbE throughput without SFP+ cabling.
 Power: TerraMaster rates it at 45 W under read and write load and 14 W in hibernation. Warranty is 2 years.
 Buy it direct, not on Amazon. The same N305 model costs about $595 on the TerraMaster store against about $700 on Amazon, a gap of about $105. There is also no PCIe slot, so 5GbE is the ceiling for the life of the box.
 Check price on Amazon 
 5. UniFi UNAS Pro 4: best Hyper Backup and Time Machine target
 UniFi UNAS Pro 4: 4 bays, 2x 10G SFP+, 8 GB RAM, 1U. Image: Ubiquiti. 
 UNAS is a file and backup appliance, and that is the right way to judge it. UniFi Drive serves SMB and NFS, acts as a Time Machine target, backs up to another UNAS, an SMB server, Backblaze B2, S3 or Wasabi, and since version 4.2.2 it can pull data from a remote rsync server, which includes a DiskStation. It suits a UniFi network with a rack, where the Synology keeps running apps and the UNAS takes the backups, or where the apps move to a mini PC.
 CPU and memory: quad Cortex-A57 at 2.0 GHz with 8 GB RAM, neither upgradeable nor ECC.
 Storage: four bays with RAID 5, 6 or 10, and two M.2 slots that work as cache only.
 Network: two 10G SFP+ ports plus one 1GbE port, in a 1U chassis.
 Price: about $549 at store.ui.com with the surcharge included ($499 before it), with a 2-year warranty when bought direct.
 Not for app hosting. UniFi Drive has no Docker, no virtual machines, no app store, no Plex and no desktop sync client. Amazon listings for every UNAS model come from third-party resellers at roughly 13% to 89% over the surcharge-included store price. An authorised reseller purchase carries a 1-year warranty instead of 2, and Ubiquiti gives none at all on units from unauthorised sellers, so buy direct. For a desktop backup box, the UNAS 2 costs about $219 but supports RAID 1 only.
 Check price at store.ui.com 
 6. DIY TrueNAS or Unraid in a Jonsbo N3: best for control
 Jonsbo N3: eight 3.5-inch bays plus one 2.5-inch, mini-ITX, SFX power supply. Image: Jonsbo. 
 A DIY build removes the vendor OS from the decision. TrueNAS Community Edition is free and replaces Snapshot Replication with native ZFS snapshots and replication, while the Unraid array is the closest DIY equivalent to SHR: drives of any size, with parity at least as large as the largest data drive. Unraid licences cost $49 (Starter, 6 devices), $109 (Unleashed) or $249 (Lifetime). The TrueNAS vs Unraid comparison covers which one fits which workload.
 Case: the Jonsbo N3 holds eight 3.5-inch drives and one 2.5-inch drive, takes mini-ITX boards and SFX power supplies up to 105 mm, and fits a 130 mm CPU cooler.
 Board: Intel N150 six-SATA ITX boards are the common pairing, but their six SATA ports share an ASM1166 controller on one PCIe 3.0 lane, and NASCompares measured about 650 MB/s across six drives on a CWWK board with that layout. That is enough for hard drives behind 2.5GbE and too slow for an SSD array.
 Memory: N150 boards advertise up to 48 GB on one SODIMM, while Intel lists 16 GB as the supported maximum.
 Support is the cost. A DIY box has a warranty per part and no vendor to call, and the build itself takes an afternoon. The DIY NAS vs prebuilt cost comparison prices the full build against a DS425+, and the NAS case guide lists alternatives to the N3.
 Check price on Amazon 
 DSM app replacement map
 “Docker” means a self-hosted container you deploy and update yourself; “none” means no native or catalogued equivalent was found. The rows are ordered by how often each DSM app is the reason an owner stays.
 DSM app UGOS Pro (UGREEN) QTS / QuTS hero (QNAP) UniFi Drive (UNAS) TrueNAS / Unraid 
 Active Backup for Business (PCs) File-level PC backup; no bare-metal image documented HDP PC Agent, free, bare-metal restore none Docker: UrBackup 
 Active Backup (VMs) none HDP for PC/VM, VMware and Hyper-V none none native 
 Active Backup for Microsoft 365 none HDP for SaaS, free for 30 users OneDrive backup, work and school accounts only none native 
 Synology Photos Photos QuMagie iPhone backup through UniFi Endpoint, no library Immich 
 Synology Drive Desktop client with sync Qsync File access only, no sync client Docker: Nextcloud or Syncthing 
 Hyper Backup Sync & Backup (rsync based) HBS 3 Backup to UNAS, SMB, B2, S3, Wasabi Cloud Sync tasks, rsync, ZFS replication 
 Snapshot Replication Snapshots on Btrfs pools Snapshots; immutable on QuTS hero h6.0 Snapshots ZFS snapshots and replication 
 Surveillance Station none listed QVR Pro, 8 channels free; playback past 14 days paid none (UniFi Protect runs on a separate NVR) Docker: Frigate 
 Container Manager Docker Container Station none Native apps (Docker) 
 Virtual Machine Manager Virtual Machine Virtualization Station none Native VMs 
 QuickConnect UGREENlink myQNAPcloud UniFi Site Manager Tailscale app 
 SHR none, fixed RAID levels none, fixed RAID levels none, fixed RAID levels Unraid array (mixed sizes); TrueNAS RAIDZ expansion adds disks but not mixed sizes 
 Time Machine Yes Yes Yes Yes 
 Two rows decide most migrations. An office that images Windows PCs with Active Backup has one appliance replacement: HDP on QNAP. A household that relies on SHR to grow storage one drive at a time has TRAID on TerraMaster or a DIY Unraid build, and nothing else on this list.
 Moving the data off a DiskStation
 No vendor ships a one-click Synology importer. UGREEN, QNAP and UniFi all document the same path: run rsync between the two boxes and recreate users, shares and apps by hand. The UGREEN migration guide states the limit directly: users, applications, snapshots and platform metadata do not migrate, and that includes photo albums and face tags.
 Step 1: Copy with rsync, not a Hyper Backup archive
 A Hyper Backup task writes .hbk archives that only Hyper Backup, Hyper Backup Explorer or Hyper Backup Vault can read. For a migration, either enable the rsync service in DSM under Control Panel > File Services > rsync and pull from the new box (UGOS Pro and UniFi Drive 4.2.2 or newer both support a pull), or, for a QNAP target, run the HBS 3 rsync server and create a Hyper Backup task with the “rsync copy (single-version)” destination, which writes plain files.
 Step 2: Keep the old disks readable
 Leave the Synology disks untouched until the copy is verified. If the DiskStation fails mid-migration, the Synology PC recovery procedure reads an SHR or classic RAID volume on Ubuntu: install mdadm and lvm2 , assemble with mdadm -AsfR , activate with vgchange -ay , and mount the volume read-only. It does not apply to volumes with a read-write SSD cache, so remove that cache on the DiskStation before the move.
 Step 3: Do not move the disks into the new NAS
 SHR disks cannot be imported into UGOS Pro, QTS, TOS or UniFi Drive. The new box initialises its own pool, which wipes the drives, so the migration needs enough new capacity to hold a full copy. With a WD Red Plus 12 TB at about $460 on Amazon at the time of writing, four of them cost about $1,842, more than any 4-bay box in this guide; the NAS hard drive guide tracks current CMR prices by capacity.

 Data to copy 1GbE (110 MB/s) 2.5GbE (280 MB/s) 10GbE, source array at 500 MB/s

 The table assumes sustained large-file throughput: 110 MB/s is the practical ceiling of 1GbE, 280 MB/s of 2.5GbE, and 500 MB/s is an assumed sequential rate for a four-drive hard disk array rather than a 10GbE limit. A photo library with millions of small files runs well below these figures, and rsync over SSH can be CPU-bound on a J4125 below the 2.5GbE figure. The column that matters is set by the slower box: a DS925+ or DS425+ has no 10GbE option, so a copy from either one tops out at the 2.5GbE column whatever the destination supports. Synology vs Ugreen 2026: Which NAS Actually Wins?

 Synology vs Ugreen 2026: Which NAS Actually Wins?
 Updated: 2026-07-02 · Last verified July 2026 
 TL;DR Synology still has the best NAS software (DSM is polished and mature), but its 2025 drive policy on the new Plus models cost it the automatic-default status it held for a decade. Ugreen's NASync line matches or beats Synology on hardware for a similar price, ships with 10 GbE on the popular DXP4800 Plus, and doesn't lock which HDDs or NVMe SSDs you can install. If you want plug-and-play family storage and can live with the compatibility list, Synology is still a fine buy; if you want more raw hardware, container flexibility, and no vendor lock-in, Ugreen is the better call in 2026.
 Synology and Ugreen aren't quite the same kind of company, and that's actually the interesting part of this comparison. Synology has spent 15 years turning polished software into a market lead, while Ugreen, better known for USB-C cables until 2024, launched into the NAS space and shipped credible hardware fast. The drive-lock episode on Synology's 2025 Plus models gave Ugreen a real opening, and by mid-2026 the choice is closer than it has ever been.
 Size the pool before you commit Compare SHR-1 vs RAID 6 on a 4-bay layout in seconds. 
 Open calculator → 
 What Synology's 2025 drive story actually changed
 The short version is that Synology tried to close its ecosystem, took heat for it, and then walked most of it back, but not all of it. On the 2025 Plus-series launch (DS225+, DS425+, DS925+, DS1825+ and siblings), the NAS units initially only accepted Synology-branded HDDs, which ended more than a decade of open drive compatibility. Wikipedia's Synology article summarizes the sequence : with the release of DSM 7.3 in October 2025 the HDD lock on 2025 units was reversed, so third-party NAS drives are again allowed on those boxes.
 What did not get reversed is the M.2 NVMe slot, which still refuses anything that isn't a Synology-branded SSD. That matters more than it sounds, because M.2 cache and M.2-as-storage-pool are two of the biggest reasons to buy a Plus model in the first place. If you want NVMe caching or a small all-flash pool, a 2025 Synology forces you into Synology's SSD prices; a Ugreen doesn't.
 Hardware: the 4-bay comparison most people are looking at
 The head-to-head that comes up most often is the Synology DS925+ against the Ugreen NASync DXP4800 Plus . Both are 4-bay boxes aimed at homelab and small-office use, and their spec sheets illustrate the whole story of this comparison.
 The DS925+ is a 4-bay AMD Ryzen box with 4 GB of RAM out of the box and two 2.5 GbE ports for networking. It's a modest hardware bill on paper, but Synology's argument has always been that DSM makes up the difference, and for most household workloads it genuinely does. The DXP4800 Plus is a 4-bay Intel box with 8 GB of DDR5 RAM (expandable), 10 GbE built in, a 2.5 GbE second port, two M.2 NVMe slots without brand restrictions, and a PCIe slot for later expansion. On paper the Ugreen has more of everything that matters for the next five years of the box's life.
 The one hardware note that goes the other way is memory type: Synology's Plus boxes have historically used ECC RAM, which is genuinely valuable if you're running ZFS-like workloads because ECC memory catches single-bit errors before they get written to disk . For a family NAS this is a nice-to-have rather than a make-or-break, but power users planning a big pool will still weight it.
 Software: DSM leads, UGOS Pro is closing the gap
 DSM is still the most polished NAS OS you can buy in 2026. Snapshots, Hyper Backup, Active Backup for Business, and Surveillance Station are the sort of things you notice most when you switch away: the day-to-day workflows are quicker and better documented than anything else in the category. Container Manager gives you Docker without leaving the DSM UI, and Virtual Machine Manager runs full VMs on the Plus models with enough RAM.
 UGOS Pro isn't at that level yet, but it has closed a meaningful part of the gap since Ugreen launched the NASync line. Docker is integrated, snapshots work, and the built-in photos, files, and backup apps do the basics well. What UGOS Pro doesn't have is a first-party VMM equivalent, and the app ecosystem is thinner than Synology's, with fewer third-party integrations and community packages. For a technical user comfortable with Docker Compose files this is barely a limitation; for someone who wants a shrink-wrapped experience, DSM is still ahead.
 Drive freedom and what it means for your build
 The practical impact of Synology's remaining restrictions is easiest to see through a concrete build. If you want a 4-bay Plus model plus NVMe cache in 2026, you either buy the Synology-branded NVMe SSDs or you go without cache; third-party NVMe still isn't accepted for storage-pool use on the 2025 boxes. On the HDD side you're fine again after DSM 7.3, but you'll still want to cross-check Synology's compatibility list for whichever drive you're planning to buy so you don't hit a warning banner in DSM.
 Ugreen doesn't play that game. Every CMR NAS-grade HDD and every mainstream M.2 NVMe SSD just works. That's the ecosystem argument in one sentence: you keep the freedom to shop drive-by-drive on price and warranty, without a vendor telling you which SKU is "supported" for the feature you already paid for.

 An honest cost picture
 Prices move too much to quote a euro figure that will still be right next week, so it's worth spelling out how to think about the total-cost picture rather than the sticker. On the DS925+ side the NAS is only part of the equation; if you want NVMe caching you're paying Synology's SSD tax on top, and if you buy Synology's own HAT3300/HAT5300 HDDs to avoid all compatibility warnings you're paying a small premium there too. On the DXP4800 Plus you can shop for HDDs and NVMe SSDs by price-per-terabyte and warranty on any given day, which is where the real savings tend to come from over a 3-5 year hold. For the drive picks themselves, our roundup of the best NAS drives in 2026 and the more careful look at disk failure statistics are the two things worth reading before you order.
 When Synology still makes sense
 DSM is genuinely excellent, and there are households where its polish is worth more than any hardware advantage on the other side. If someone else in the family will run the NAS and you want the experience to look and feel like a consumer appliance, DSM's photo apps, Time Machine support, and the Surveillance Station bundle add up to a very smooth first setup. Long support windows are another Synology strength: the DSM update cadence is steady and predictable, and older Plus models continue to receive meaningful updates years after launch. The trade-off is that you're accepting the drive policy Synology has settled on, so plan your NVMe pool accordingly.
 When Ugreen is the better pick
 For anyone comfortable with a Docker container or a Compose file, the DXP4800 Plus is the more interesting box in 2026. You get 10 GbE without paying for an add-in card, DDR5 that you can expand yourself, two M.2 NVMe slots you can populate with whichever SSDs you want, and a PCIe slot for later. UGOS Pro will occasionally show that it's the younger platform, but for the price-per-hardware-slot you're getting, it's a straightforward win. If you're planning to run Jellyfin or Plex , self-host services, or do anything remotely developer-adjacent, this is the one to buy.
 Where other platforms fit around this
 Two names come up often enough to mention. QNAP sits between Synology and Ugreen on hardware value and has the most feature-heavy OS of the three, but its security history over the last several years has been rougher than either of the others, worth considering if you'll keep the box behind a firewall and never expose it to the public internet. DIY with Unraid or TrueNAS gives you the widest hardware range and the highest ceiling, at the cost of doing the setup yourself; our Unraid vs TrueNAS vs OpenMediaVault and Synology vs QNAP vs DIY comparisons go deeper on the trade-offs.
 Ubiquiti sits further out again. The UniFi UNAS line starts at $199 and puts a 10-gigabit SFP+ port into a $499 seven-bay chassis, hardware neither Synology nor Ugreen matches at that price, but UniFi Drive is storage software with no Docker, no virtual machines and no Plex. Against Ugreen in particular that is the entire decision, because Ugreen sells you an Intel box precisely so you can run things on it and UniFi sells you the opposite bargain. If you already run UniFi switches and want files and backups in the same console, it is a serious option. If the reason you are reading a Synology versus Ugreen comparison is the app ecosystem, UniFi is not in the running.
 Recommendation
 If you want a shrink-wrapped experience for the family and you're happy to stay within Synology's drive list, the DS925+ (or the DS224+ if you only need two bays) is still a very safe buy. If you want the best hardware for the money, the ability to shop drives freely, and you're planning to grow into 10 GbE or self-hosting, the Ugreen DXP4800 Plus is the current best-value pick in the mainstream 4-bay class. Everything else (QNAP for feature depth, DIY for maximum flexibility) is a legitimate answer to a more specific question, but for the general "Synology or Ugreen?" prompt, that's the honest split in 2026.
 Frequently asked questions
 Which is better: Synology or Ugreen in 2026? Synology still has the most polished NAS software with DSM, so it's the safer pick for a plug-and-play family setup. Ugreen offers more hardware per euro on the DXP4800 Plus, ships with 10 GbE, and doesn't restrict which HDDs or NVMe SSDs you can install, which makes it the better call for tech-savvy users.
 Are Synology's 2025 drive restrictions still in effect? The HDD lock on the 2025 Plus models was reversed with DSM 7.3 in October 2025, so third-party NAS drives are again allowed. The M.2 NVMe slot remains locked to Synology-branded SSDs, which matters if you plan to run NVMe cache or an M.2 storage pool.
 Has Ugreen UGOS Pro caught up to Synology DSM? UGOS Pro has closed a meaningful part of the gap since the NASync launch: Docker is integrated, snapshots work, and the built-in photos, files, and backup apps cover the basics. What's still missing is a first-party VMM equivalent and Synology's depth of third-party apps.

A network-attached storage (NAS) box used to be a thing only IT hobbyists owned. In 2026 it is closer to a household appliance: a small always-on computer with hard drive bays that stores your files, streams your media, and runs the little services that keep a connected home humming. But "best home NAS" is a trick question, because the right pick depends entirely on what you plan to do with it.

This guide skips the spec-sheet overload and organizes the decision around how real people actually use a NAS at home. We will look at who genuinely needs one, walk through three common scenarios, and name a best pick for each.

Who Needs This?

You probably want a NAS if any of these sound like you. First, you are tired of juggling external USB drives and cloud subscriptions and want one private place for everything. Second, you take a lot of photos and video and have outgrown free cloud tiers. Third, you want to stream your own movie and music collection to TVs and phones around the house without monthly streaming fees. Fourth, you want automatic, redundant backups of multiple computers so a single drive failure never costs you data.

You probably do not need one if you own a single laptop, store little, and are happy paying for a cloud plan. For that life, a USB SSD plus cloud sync is simpler and cheaper. A NAS earns its keep when you have multiple devices, multiple people, or a growing media library. If that is you, browse current models on the Newegg NAS selection to see what fits your budget.

Use-Case Scenarios

Scenario 1: Simple backup and photo vault. You want a reliable, low-effort place to back up two or three computers and offload your phone's photo roll. You are not running heavy apps and you do not stream much. Here, two drive bays in a mirror (RAID 1) are plenty, low power draw matters, and ease of setup beats raw horsepower.

Scenario 2: Plex / Jellyfin media server. You have a movie, TV, and music library and want to stream it to TVs, tablets, and phones, sometimes to several screens at once. The deciding factor is the processor and whether it has hardware transcoding and an HDMI port, plus enough bays to hold a large library that keeps growing.

Scenario 3: Power-user home server. You want to run Docker containers, virtual machines, smart-home dashboards, a personal cloud, and maybe self-hosted apps, all at once. You need a strong CPU, generous and upgradable RAM, fast 2.5GbE or 10GbE networking, and NVMe slots for caching.

Best Pick per Scenario

Best for simple backup: Synology DS224+. This is the friendly entry point. It is a 2-bay unit built around a quad-core Intel Celeron at 2.0 GHz with 2GB of DDR4 (expandable to 6GB). Synology's DSM software is the easiest in the category, and its Active Backup and Photos apps handle exactly the "back up my computers and phone" job this scenario describes. Two bays in RAID 1 give you redundancy without overspending. It is available on Newegg, with MSRP around $370 (commonly sold lower).

Best for media server: UGREEN NASync DXP4800 Plus. For Plex and Jellyfin, this 4-bay unit punches above its price. It runs an Intel Pentium Gold 8505 (a 5-core 12th-gen chip with quick-sync hardware transcoding), ships with 8GB of DDR5, and crucially pairs one 10GbE port with one 2.5GbE port plus a 4K-capable HDMI output. Four bays support up to roughly 144TB of raw capacity, with two NVMe slots for caching. Expect a price around $620, available on Newegg. If you prefer the most polished media app ecosystem instead, the QNAP TS-464 (quad-core Celeron N5095/N5105, 8GB DDR4, HDMI 2.1, dual 2.5GbE) is a strong alternative, available on Newegg.

Best for power-user home server: Synology DS925+ or TerraMaster F4-424 Pro. If you live in the Synology ecosystem and want rock-solid software for Docker, Virtual Machine Manager, and surveillance, the DS925+ is the pick: a 4-bay unit with a quad-core AMD Ryzen V1500B, 4GB ECC DDR4 expandable to 32GB, dual 2.5GbE, and two M.2 slots. MSRP is about $620, available on Newegg. If you want the most raw compute for the money and are comfortable with TerraMaster's TOS software, the F4-424 Pro is a beast for the class: an 8-core Intel Core i3-N305, 32GB of DDR5, four bays, and dual 2.5GbE, with a US price around $699, available on Newegg. The Synology wins on software polish; the TerraMaster wins on horsepower per dollar.

The Drives Matter Too

Whichever enclosure you choose, remember that most home NAS units ship diskless, so you buy the hard drives separately. For an always-on box, use drives rated for 24/7 NAS duty rather than standard desktop drives. You can compare capacities and warranties across the Newegg NAS hard drive selection and plan to fill at least two bays so you can run a mirror from day one.

Verdict

There is no single best home NAS for 2026, only the best one for your scenario. If you just want painless backups and a private photo library, the Synology DS224+ is the easy, affordable answer. If your home revolves around streaming your own media, the UGREEN NASync DXP4800 Plus delivers transcoding muscle and fast networking at a fair price. And if you are the household tinkerer running containers and virtual machines, step up to the Synology DS925+ for software polish or the TerraMaster F4-424 Pro for sheer performance. Match the box to the job, add NAS-rated drives, and you will have a private cloud that pays for itself in a year or two.

A NAS is worth it if you have multiple devices or people, a growing photo and video library, or want automatic redundant backups and private media streaming. If you own a single laptop and are happy with a cloud plan, a USB SSD plus cloud sync is simpler and cheaper.

In this NASCompares software comparison, we look at whether Synology DSM is still the benchmark for turnkey NAS software and where QNAP, UGREEN, UniFi, TerraMaster and ASUSTOR now stand in 2026.
 Quick Answer: Is Synology DSM Still the Best NAS Software in 2026? 
 For most turnkey NAS buyers, Synology DSM is still the most polished and consistent NAS operating system in 2026. It remains the platform that feels the easiest to recommend to less technical home users, small offices and buyers who want a NAS to feel like a finished appliance rather than a project. However, that does not mean DSM is the best answer for every buyer. QNAP, UGREEN, UniFi, TerraMaster and ASUSTOR now offer very different strengths, and in several areas they can make more sense than Synology depending on the workload.
 The practical takeaway is this: choose DSM if smooth software, mature first-party apps and low-friction management are the priority. Choose an alternative if you care more about ZFS flexibility, third-party OS freedom, lower-cost hardware, network ecosystem integration, or a brand that is currently moving faster in specific software areas such as AI search, storage tiering or hardware openness.
 IMPORTANT CONTEXT – This is a software/platform comparison, not a single NAS model review. 
Features, update timing and app availability can vary by model, region and firmware generation. DSM 7.4, TOS 7 and other 2026 software changes should be checked against each vendor’s official release notes before making a business-critical purchase decision.

 What This Comparison Covers and What It Does Not 
 This comparison focuses on turnkey NAS platforms from established NAS hardware brands. That means Synology DSM, QNAP QTS/QuTS hero, UGREEN UGOS, UniFi NAS OS, TerraMaster TOS and ASUSTOR ADM. It does not directly compare TrueNAS, Unraid, ZimaOS or other install-it-yourself NAS operating systems, because those are a different buying decision: you are choosing both software and a DIY/bring-your-own-hardware route.
 That distinction matters. A turnkey NAS buyer usually wants a supported appliance with vendor updates, mobile apps, backup tools, file management and storage configuration all tied together. A DIY NAS buyer may be happier trading simplicity for control. This article is about the former.
 Synology DSM 7.4 sets the context for comparing turnkey NAS software platforms in 2026. 
 Synology DSM: Still the Smoothest Turnkey NAS Experience 
 Synology DSM remains the standard that most NAS software is measured against. It is not always the fastest-moving platform, and it is not always the most flexible, but DSM still wins on interface consistency, mature first-party applications and the feeling that the NAS is an appliance rather than a collection of utilities.
 For home users, photographers, small businesses and less technical buyers, that polish matters. Synology Drive, Photos, Active Backup, Hyper Backup, Surveillance Station and the wider DSM package ecosystem are familiar, well documented and generally cohesive. DSM is also the platform most likely to make a first-time NAS owner feel comfortable quickly.
 The counterpoint is that Synology’s direction has become more controlled in recent years. Hardware compatibility, enterprise focus, slower adoption of some newer features and questions around future DSM direction all mean it is worth looking over the fence before assuming DSM is automatically the answer.
 Synology DSM release notes remain the best place to verify current DSM update availability and fixes.
 QNAP QuTS Hero: More Flexible, More Powerful, Less Polished 
 QNAP remains the closest long-term Synology rival in software depth, but the pitch is different. QNAP gives users more control, more hardware variety, ZFS through QuTS hero, Qtier-style storage tiering, broader network and expansion options, and more willingness to experiment with AI, containers, virtualisation and performance features.
 The trade-off is complexity. QNAP can be a better platform for enthusiasts, SMB admins and users who know exactly what they want from storage architecture, but it is not usually as calm or smooth as DSM. The interface has improved, and QNAP has strengthened security after well-publicised historic incidents, but new buyers should still plan a proper security and backup configuration rather than treating any NAS as safe by default.
 QNAP QuTS hero remains the more flexible and ZFS-focused DSM alternative, with extra complexity. 
 QNAP’s current software story is strongest when you want features DSM does not prioritise in the same way: ZFS-based QuTS hero, inline compression/deduplication options where appropriate, richer storage configuration, AI search and more flexible app/service deployment. QNAP’s Qsirch page, for example, now promotes keyword, semantic and RAG-style search capabilities for NAS data. See QNAP Qsirch .
 UGREEN UGOS Pro: The Fastest-Rising DSM-Style Alternative 
 UGREEN is the newest major name in this group for Western NAS buyers, and UGOS Pro is clearly trying to deliver a DSM-like user experience with modern hardware and aggressive pricing. For simple storage, photos, video, music, mobile apps, file browsing and backup basics, UGOS has become much more credible than many expected.
 The biggest caveat is maturity. UGREEN has not had the same decade-plus public security testing, enterprise deployment history or long-term software scrutiny as Synology and QNAP. The interface is friendly and the hardware can be compelling, but administrators should still treat it as a younger platform and verify security controls, MFA, backup tools, encryption scope and update cadence for their use case.
 UGREEN UGOS is one of the newest DSM-style NAS software platforms, with strong usability but maturing security depth. 
 One UGREEN advantage is openness on many models: the ability to run third-party operating systems is attractive for users who may start with UGOS but later switch to TrueNAS, Unraid or another platform. That makes UGREEN hardware more flexible than a locked appliance, even if UGOS itself is still catching up in some areas. UGREEN’s UGOS Pro page lists its current official software feature set.
 UniFi UNAS: Great If You Want Storage, Not a Full NAS App Store 
 UniFi NAS is the most focused platform here. If you already live inside the UniFi ecosystem and want shared storage that fits into that network management experience, UNAS makes sense. It is simple, affordable and storage-first.
 That is also the limitation. UniFi NAS is not trying to match Synology package-for-package. There is no broad multimedia suite, no deep NAS app ecosystem in the traditional Synology/QNAP sense, and many workloads that other NAS platforms handle internally may need to be offloaded to mini PCs, servers or other clients. If you want clean storage inside a UniFi environment, that is a strength. If you want an all-in-one NAS application platform, it is a weakness.
 TerraMaster TOS 7: The Underdog Is Getting Much More Serious 
 TerraMaster has improved significantly, and TOS 7 is the clearest sign that the company knows software polish is now just as important as hardware value. TOS 7 brings a more modern interface and a broader set of features, including WORM-style controls, iSCSI, security scanning, file management, backup tools and multimedia applications.
 The caution is that TOS 7 still needs to prove itself over time. TerraMaster has been in the NAS market for years, but it competes against larger vendors and also against cheaper emerging NAS brands. The positive view is that TOS is evolving quickly and becoming much more credible. The cautious view is that buyers should check current firmware status, app support and real-world stability before deploying it for business-critical data.
 ASUSTOR ADM: Consistent, Capable and a Little Conservative 
 ASUSTOR ADM is easy to underestimate. It may not always have the newest-looking interface or the most headline-grabbing apps, but it covers the fundamentals well: file services, security scanning, iSCSI, containers, virtual machines, multimedia, WORM, encryption options and a consistent interface across the platform.
 The criticism is that parts of ADM can feel dated compared with newer-looking DSM, UGOS and TOS 7 experiences. The praise is that ASUSTOR has kept the platform consistent and has also supported ideas such as third-party OS flexibility and hardware openness earlier than some rivals. For users who value stable fundamentals and do not need the most polished photo or AI app experience, ADM still deserves a place on the shortlist.

 Security and Backups Matter More Than Brand Loyalty 
 One of the most important points in any NAS software comparison is that no platform should be trusted blindly. Synology, QNAP, TerraMaster, UGREEN, UniFi and ASUSTOR all need proper configuration: strong passwords, MFA where available, limited exposure to the internet, regular updates, snapshots where appropriate, and a backup plan that is not just “the NAS has RAID”.
 NAS software choice can reduce friction, but it cannot replace good administration. If a system is holding business data, family media, client files or irreplaceable archives, then backup, recovery testing and access control should come before debates about which interface looks best.

 Frequently Asked Questions 
 Is Synology DSM still the best NAS software in 2026? 
 For most turnkey NAS users, yes. DSM is still the most polished and cohesive NAS software platform. However, QNAP, UGREEN, UniFi, TerraMaster and ASUSTOR can be better choices for specific priorities such as ZFS, price, hardware openness or UniFi ecosystem integration.
 Is QNAP better than Synology for advanced users? 
 Often, yes. QNAP generally offers more flexibility, broader hardware options and QuTS hero with ZFS on supported systems. The trade-off is that QNAP is usually more complex and less streamlined than DSM.
 Is UGREEN UGOS Pro a serious DSM alternative? 
 UGREEN UGOS Pro is becoming a serious option for users who want a clean, DSM-like experience and strong hardware value. It is still a younger platform, so security maturity, update cadence and business deployment requirements should be checked carefully.
 Is UniFi UNAS a full replacement for Synology DSM? 
 Not for everyone. UniFi UNAS is best treated as a storage-first platform for UniFi users, not as a full app-rich DSM replacement. It is appealing if you want simple shared storage inside a UniFi network.
 Is TerraMaster TOS 7 ready for everyday NAS users? 
 TOS 7 is a major improvement and makes TerraMaster more competitive, but buyers should check the current firmware state, app support and stability for their exact model before relying on it for critical data.
 Is ASUSTOR ADM outdated? 
 ADM can look less modern than some newer platforms, but it remains consistent, capable and feature-complete for many users. It is worth considering if you value fundamentals, containers, VM support, security tools and hardware openness.
 Which NAS software is best for Plex? 
 Plex depends heavily on the NAS hardware as well as software. Synology is easy to use, QNAP and ASUSTOR often provide broader hardware/transcoding choices, and UGREEN may offer strong modern hardware value. Always check the exact CPU/GPU and Plex compatibility before buying.
 Should I choose NAS software based only on the interface? 
 No. Interface polish matters, but backup tools, security controls, snapshots, app support, hardware compatibility, update history and recovery options matter more for long-term data safety.

Best Home NAS Drives of 2026 
 A home NAS is the simplest way to stop paying for cloud storage and keep your photos, backups, and media on drives you own. The catch in 2026 is that the box is only part of the bill — every pick here is sold diskless, so budget for NAS hard drives on top. Every price below was verified as of October 30, 2026. Two warnings up front: Synology's current models no longer transcode video in hardware, and 4-bay prices have been moving week to week.
 Quick picks
 Synology DS925+ — Best overall: the most polished software here, ECC memory, and room to grow to nine bays
 Synology DS225+ — Best for beginners: a simple, quiet 2-bay starter NAS with the same easy DSM software
 UGREEN NASync DXP4800 Plus — Best for Plex and media: Intel graphics for hardware transcoding, plus a 10GbE port
 QNAP TS-464 — Best for power users: a PCIe expansion slot, HDMI output, and the deepest settings of any pick here
 TerraMaster F4-425 Plus — Best hardware value: 16GB of DDR5 and dual 5GbE for less than the other 4-bay boxes
 How we picked
 Software first: the OS decides how easy backups, photos, and remote access feel day to day
 Drive bays and RAID: 2 bays for simple mirroring, 4 bays for RAID 5 and room to grow
 Networking speed: 2.5GbE is the floor; faster ports matter for large files
 Media transcoding: whether the chip converts video in hardware for Plex or Jellyfin
 Current, verified pricing: prices checked October 30, 2026, drives always costed separately
 Synology DS925+ — Best overall
 The DS925+ is the 4-bay to buy if you want the software to disappear into the background. Synology's DSM remains the most polished NAS operating system: backups for PCs and Macs, a strong photos app, file sync, snapshots, and surveillance tools all work without much tinkering. The hardware backs that up — an AMD Ryzen V1500B quad-core processor, 4GB of ECC memory expandable to 32GB, two 2.5GbE ports, and two M.2 slots for SSD cache. Two caveats: the Ryzen chip has no graphics engine, so it cannot transcode video in hardware for Plex (pick the UGREEN below for that), and Synology pricing has been volatile — listings moved between roughly $640 and $770 through October, so check the live price before you buy.
 Standout features: 
 4 bays, expandable to 9 with a Synology expansion unit; two M.2 NVMe slots for cache
 4GB ECC DDR4 memory, expandable to 32GB — ECC protects against silent memory errors
 Dual 2.5GbE ports; DSM software with backup, photos, sync, and surveillance apps
 Price & where to buy: $765 at Amazon, as of October 30, 2026 — amazon.com (diskless; confirm the price at checkout)
 Who it's for: Households and home offices that want the easiest, best-supported software and room to grow.
 Synology DS225+ — Best for beginners
 The DS225+ is the starter version of the same idea: two drive bays, the same DSM software, and a much lower price. Set the drives up as a mirrored pair and a single drive failure costs you nothing but a replacement disk. It runs an Intel Celeron J4125 with 2GB of memory (expandable to 6GB), has 2.5GbE and 1GbE ports, and sips power — a good fit for a box that stays on around the clock.
 The limits are predictable: capacity tops out at whatever two drives hold, there are no M.2 slots, and Synology has disabled GPU access in DSM on this generation, so it does not hardware-transcode for Plex despite the Intel chip. For backups, photos, and file sharing, none of that matters.
 Standout features: 
 2 bays with mirrored (RAID 1) protection; up to 40TB raw with two 20TB drives
 Same DSM software as the DS925+ — backups, Synology Photos, file sync, and snapshots
 Low power draw and a 2.5GbE port, so transfers are not stuck at gigabit speeds
 Price & where to buy: $364.99 at Amazon, as of October 30, 2026 — amazon.com (diskless)
 Who it's for: First-time NAS buyers who want simple, reliable backup and photo storage.
 UGREEN NASync DXP4800 Plus — Best for Plex and media
 The DXP4800 Plus is the media-server pick, because it does the one thing the current Synology boxes cannot: hardware transcoding. Its Intel Pentium Gold 8505 has integrated graphics that convert video on the fly for Plex and Jellyfin, so films play smoothly on phones and TVs that cannot handle the original file. The rest of the hardware is a step up, too — 8GB of DDR5 (expandable to 64GB), 10GbE and 2.5GbE ports, two M.2 slots, a built-in 128GB system SSD, and 4K HDMI output.
 UGREEN's UGOS Pro software is younger than DSM and QTS, with a smaller app catalog, but it covers the home essentials — backups, photos, Docker, and virtual machines — and accepts standard third-party drives without compatibility-list friction.
 Standout features: 
 Intel Pentium Gold 8505 with integrated graphics — hardware transcoding for Plex and Jellyfin
 10GbE + 2.5GbE networking, the fastest built-in ports in this roundup
 8GB DDR5 (up to 64GB), two M.2 slots, 128GB system SSD, and 4K HDMI output
 Price & where to buy: $656.99 at Amazon, as of October 30, 2026 — amazon.com (diskless; list price $729.99)
 Who it's for: Anyone building a Plex or Jellyfin server, plus creators who move large video files and can use 10GbE.
 QNAP TS-464 — Best for power users
 The TS-464 is the tinkerer's 4-bay. Beyond the expected two M.2 slots and dual 2.5GbE ports, it adds two things no other pick here offers: a PCIe slot, so you can add a 10GbE card later, and an HDMI output for running media straight to a TV. Its Intel Celeron N5095 has integrated graphics for hardware transcoding, it ships with 8GB of memory (up to 16GB), and QNAP's QTS exposes more settings and virtualization options than DSM does.
 That depth cuts both ways — QTS takes more learning than Synology's software, and beginners will use a fraction of it.
 Standout features: 
 PCIe expansion slot — add 10GbE networking or more storage later
 Intel Celeron N5095 with integrated graphics for hardware transcoding; HDMI output
 8GB RAM, two M.2 NVMe slots, and dual 2.5GbE ports
 Price & where to buy: $639 at Amazon, as of October 30, 2026 — amazon.com (diskless; it was $509 during the October Prime event)
 Who it's for: Power users who want expansion options, virtual machines, and the deepest settings menu in a home NAS.
 TerraMaster F4-425 Plus — Best hardware value
 The F4-425 Plus wins on the spec sheet per dollar. For less than every other 4-bay pick here you get an Intel N150 processor, 16GB of DDR5 fitted as standard, dual 5GbE ports, and three M.2 slots — one more than anyone else — usable for SSD storage pools as well as cache. TerraMaster's TRAID mode is genuinely handy, too: it mixes different-sized drives more efficiently than classic RAID, so you can start with drives you already own.
 The trade-off is software polish: TOS is functional for backups, media, and Docker, but less refined than DSM or QTS, with a smaller app ecosystem. If you will trade a slicker interface for stronger hardware for less money, this is the value end of the 4-bay market.
 Standout features: 
 16GB DDR5 included — double or quadruple what the other 4-bay picks ship with
 Dual 5GbE ports and three M.2 slots for cache or SSD storage pools
 TRAID flexible RAID makes good use of mixed-size drives; up to 144TB total capacity
 Price & where to buy: $599.99 at the TerraMaster Store, as of October 30, 2026 — terra-master.com (diskless)
 Who it's for: Budget-minded enthusiasts who want the strongest hardware for the money and do not mind a less polished operating system.
 Bottom line
 Start with how many drives you need. For simple, set-and-forget backup, the DS225+ at $364.99 is enough for most homes. For a 4-bay that will last, the DS925+ at $765 has the best software and ECC memory — unless you stream with Plex, in which case the UGREEN DXP4800 Plus at $656.99 is the right pick and costs less. Power users should look at the QNAP TS-464 at $639 for its PCIe slot, ideally when its sale price returns, and hardware-per-dollar shoppers should take the TerraMaster F4-425 Plus at $599.99 . And remember: the enclosure is the smaller cost — four NAS drives can cost more than the box.

 Synology is our pick for software-first buyers in 2026, and QNAP is our pick when the NAS doubles as a home-lab server. DSM, Active Backup for Business, and Synology Drive form the more integrated software stack. QNAP answers with more hardware for similar money: Intel Quick Sync for Plex, more base memory, and a PCIe slot.
 Buy a Synology DS925+ if the NAS is mainly for storage, backup, and file sync. Buy a QNAP TS-464 if you need Plex hardware transcoding, a PCIe expansion slot, or more room for containers. The two are similarly priced, so compare current prices on both before deciding.
 Software Ecosystem: DSM vs QTS
 DSM 7.4 is our preferred NAS operating system for ease of administration. Its first-party apps work together with little setup.
 Active Backup for Business backs up Windows PCs, Macs, physical servers, file servers, and virtual machines to the NAS from one console, and Active Backup for Microsoft 365 covers cloud accounts. QNAP covers similar ground with separate tools: Hybrid Backup Sync (HBS 3) for NAS-to-cloud and NAS-to-NAS jobs, and NetBak PC Agent, which gained full Windows system backup with QTS 5.2. Synology’s suite is the more integrated of the two.
 Synology Drive is a mature self-hosted alternative to Dropbox, with sync, versioning, and sharing. QNAP’s equivalent, Qsync, covers the same basics; we think Synology Drive is the more refined of the two.
 DSM 7.3 added Synology Tiering for moving rarely used data to cheaper storage, custom data masking in the AI Console before data reaches third-party AI services, and enhanced file locking in Synology Drive. QTS 5.2 added Security Center, which watches for unusual file activity and can respond with protective measures such as backups or blocking, plus a kernel-mode SMB daemon that QNAP says helps most on all-flash storage.
 Both platforms have mature app catalogs. DSM’s first-party apps are more consistent, while QTS offers more hardware-level options, such as HDMI output and more container types. If you live inside the NAS’s native apps, Synology wins.
 Winner: Synology. DSM is the easier OS to administer, and Active Backup is its strongest single feature.
 Hardware Value per Dollar
 This is where QNAP fights back.
 The QNAP TS-464 ships with an Intel Celeron N5095 (four cores, up to 2.9 GHz) with Intel UHD Graphics, 8 GB of DDR4, dual 2.5GbE, two M.2 NVMe slots, a PCIe Gen 3 x2 slot, and HDMI 2.1 output. The Synology DS925+ has an AMD Ryzen V1500B (four cores, eight threads), 4 GB of ECC DDR4, dual 2.5GbE, and two M.2 NVMe slots, with no PCIe slot and no HDMI.
 At similar prices, QNAP delivers more hardware. Synology’s case rests on software and ECC memory. Both are legitimate, but not every buyer needs them.
 In two bays, Synology’s current DS225+ pairs an Intel Celeron J4125 with one 2.5GbE port, one 1GbE port, and DSM, but has no M.2 slots. QNAP’s TS-264 has an Intel N5095, 8 GB of memory, dual 2.5GbE, two M.2 slots, and a PCIe Gen 3 x2 slot. QNAP’s ARM-based TS-233 is a basic two-bay for file and photo backup. If you see the previous-generation DS224+, compare it with the DS225+ on capability and lifecycle, not remaining-stock price.
 If you need 10GbE on Synology, the five-bay DS1525+ keeps the V1500B and adds a network upgrade slot for Synology’s E10G22-T1-Mini module.
 Winner: QNAP. More memory, more ports, and a PCIe slot at similar prices. Synology’s software premium is worth paying for some buyers, not all.
 Docker and Container Support
 Both brands run Docker containers capably, but the tools differ.
 Synology’s Container Manager, the successor to its Docker package, integrates tightly with DSM and gives you a clean web UI for pulling images and managing containers and networks. Common self-hosted apps such as Home Assistant, Pi-hole, Vaultwarden, and Immich publish x86-64 images that run on either brand. The DS925+‘s V1500B has eight threads and takes up to 32 GB of ECC memory, which leaves real headroom for a container-heavy build once you add RAM.
 QNAP’s Container Station is more feature-rich. It runs Docker, LXD, and Kata containers and exposes more networking options in its web UI. The TS-464’s N5095 has four threads, half the DS925+‘s eight, but a higher peak clock (2.9 GHz versus 2.2 GHz) and twice the base memory. Upgrade to 16 GB for heavier use.
 If containers become the main job, a dedicated Docker NAS or a mini PC running Proxmox is a better home for them than either appliance. For a typical home lab running a modest set of containers alongside file storage and backup, both brands handle it.
 ECC memory matters for always-on workloads. A bit flip in a database container’s memory can corrupt data silently, and Synology’s ECC support provides a real, if small, safety margin that these QNAP models lack.
 Winner: Draw. Container Station has more features; Container Manager has better DSM integration. ECC tips the scale slightly toward Synology for always-on workloads.
 Plex Transcoding
 This is QNAP’s clearest win.
 The TS-464’s Intel N5095 includes Intel UHD Graphics with Quick Sync, the hardware video engine that Plex uses for hardware-accelerated transcoding. Plex requires a Plex Pass for hardware transcoding, and its NAS notes say a Jasper Lake or newer CPU is needed to transcode reliably to HEVC. The N5095 is a Jasper Lake chip.
 The DS925+‘s AMD Ryzen V1500B has no integrated GPU, so Plex cannot use hardware transcoding on it. Every transcode runs in software on the CPU, which limits how many streams, and which formats, the NAS can convert at once. There is no fixed stream count for either box: results depend on the source codec, resolution, bitrate, HDR tone mapping, and subtitles.
 Synology’s Intel-based models, such as the two-bay DS225+ and the four-bay DS425+, both with a Celeron J4125, do have Intel graphics, but the J4125 predates Jasper Lake.
 If your Plex clients support direct play (Apple TV 4K, NVIDIA Shield, most modern smart TVs), transcoding rarely happens: the file streams from disk to the client with little CPU work. Transcoding kicks in when a client needs a different resolution, codec, or bitrate, which happens most often with phones, web browsers, and remote streams. Since April 29, 2025, Plex also requires a Plex Pass on the server owner’s account, or a Plex Pass or Remote Watch Pass on the viewer’s account, for remote video streaming of personal media.
 For households that stream to a mix of devices or share libraries with remote users, QNAP’s Intel graphics are the deciding advantage. For a single user with a modern TV, Synology works fine. Our best NAS for Plex guide covers direct-play planning and the split design where Plex runs on separate compute.
 Winner: QNAP. Intel Quick Sync versus no hardware path at all. If Plex transcoding is a primary use case, buy QNAP.
 Security Track Record
 Security is a real difference between the brands, but less lopsided than their reputations suggest. Both publish advisories ( Synology , QNAP ), and both have shipped critical fixes in the past two years.
 QNAP. QNAP devices were the target of the DeadBolt ransomware campaign in 2022, which hit internet-exposed NAS running Photo Station (advisory QSA-22-24, rated critical). In December 2024, advisory QSA-24-49 fixed eight QTS and QuTS hero flaws from Pwn2Own Ireland 2024, including an improper-authentication bug (CVE-2024-48859) and a command-injection bug (CVE-2024-50393); QNAP rated it Important. In November 2025, advisory QSA-25-45, rated critical, fixed seven QTS and QuTS hero vulnerabilities from Pwn2Own 2025.
 Synology. Synology patched critical Pwn2Own Ireland 2024 flaws in Synology Photos (Synology-SA-24:19, CVE-2024-10443) and in DSM itself (Synology-SA-24:20). In November 2025 it fixed an authentication-bypass flaw in DSM’s single sign-on from Pwn2Own 2025 (Synology-SA-25:14, rated Important).
 QTS 5.2’s Security Center, which monitors file activity for ransomware-like behavior, is a useful addition. We still give Synology the edge, mainly because QNAP’s history includes a large ransomware campaign against internet-exposed devices.
 The practical advice is the same for both brands. Do not expose the NAS management interface to the internet. Use a VPN or the vendor’s relay service (QuickConnect or myQNAPcloud) for remote access, enable automatic security updates, and disable services you do not use. QNAP’s own DeadBolt guidance was to turn off router port forwarding and use myQNAPcloud instead.
 Winner: Synology, narrowly. Both vendors ship serious fixes; QNAP’s ransomware history is the bigger warning for anyone tempted to expose a NAS to the internet.
 Mobile Apps and Remote Access
 Synology’s mobile lineup centers on Synology Photos, Synology Drive, and DS file, with DS cam for Surveillance Station. Synology Photos is free and includes facial and object recognition, which makes it a credible self-hosted alternative to Google Photos. Video Station and its DS video app are not available on DSM 7.2.2 and later, so plan on Plex, Emby, or Jellyfin for video.
 QNAP’s photo app is QuMagie, which also offers AI face and object recognition, with a QuMagie Mobile app; the older Qphoto app has reached end of life. Qfile Pro, Qsync Pro, Qvideo, and Qmusic cover files, sync, video, and music.
 For remote access, Synology’s QuickConnect and QNAP’s myQNAPcloud both provide relay-based access without router port forwarding.
 Winner: Synology, narrowly. Synology Photos and Synology Drive are more tightly integrated with DSM, although QuMagie closes most of the photo gap.
 Upgrade Paths: RAM, PCIe, and Networking
 QNAP gives you more room to grow.
 The QNAP TS-464 has a PCIe Gen 3 x2 slot that QNAP lists for optional 5GbE and 10GbE network cards. The Synology DS925+ has no PCIe slot, unlike the discontinued DS923+, so its networking tops out at the built-in dual 2.5GbE.
 If 10GbE is on your roadmap, look at the Synology DS1525+, a used or clearance DS923+, or another vendor. Do not buy the DS925+ expecting a 10GbE add-in path.
 Memory favors Synology: the DS925+ takes 32 GB of ECC DDR4 across two SO-DIMM slots, while the TS-464 tops out at 16 GB of non-ECC memory. For Docker-heavy workloads, that ceiling matters.
 Both brands sell expansion units for more drive bays. The DS925+ connects one DX525 through its USB Type-C expansion port, for nine drives in total; older Synology models such as the DS923+ use the eSATA-based DX517 instead. For the TS-464, check QNAP’s compatibility list for supported expansion enclosures.
 Winner: QNAP. The PCIe slot is a meaningful upgrade path that the DS925+ lacks. Synology wins on memory ceiling, but we think most home labs hit the network limit before the memory limit.
 Who Should Buy Which
 Buy Synology if you: 
 Prioritize ease of administration, backup tooling, and low-maintenance operation
 Use Active Backup for Business to protect Windows PCs, Macs, servers, or virtual machines
 Plan to use Synology Photos as a self-hosted Google Photos replacement
 Want ECC memory on an always-on storage server
 Mostly direct play your media
 Buy QNAP if you: 
 Run Plex and need hardware transcoding for phones, browsers, or remote users
 Want a PCIe slot for a future 5GbE or 10GbE card
 Want more hardware for similar money: twice the base memory, HDMI output, and a PCIe slot
 Want more container options (Docker, LXD, and Kata)
 Are comfortable keeping firmware updated and using a VPN for remote access
 Bottom Line
 For a NAS that is mainly file storage, backup, and a few containers, one you want to set up once and trust for years, Synology is the better brand in 2026. DSM is our preferred NAS operating system for ease of administration, and DSM 7.3 removed the biggest objection to Synology’s 2025 lineup. Since DSM 7.3 (October 2025), Synology’s 2025 Plus, Value and J models, such as the DS925+ and DS225+, accept third-party 3.5-inch HDDs and 2.5-inch SATA SSDs, but M.2 storage pools and cache still need drives on Synology’s compatibility list.
 If the NAS doubles as a home-lab server, with Plex transcoding, a PCIe network card, or a heavier container stack, the QNAP TS-464 is the better buy, which is why our 4-bay and home-lab guides pick it. Pair either with drives from our best hard drives for NAS guide, and see our 4-bay NAS comparison for model-by-model breakdowns.
 Frequently Asked Questions
 Is Synology or QNAP better for a home lab in 2026? It depends on the NAS's job. Choose Synology when it is mainly for storage, backup, and file sync, because DSM and Active Backup for Business are the most integrated software we cover. Choose QNAP when the NAS doubles as a home-lab server: the TS-464 adds Intel Quick Sync for Plex, a PCIe slot for 5GbE or 10GbE, and twice the base memory. That is why our 4-bay and home-lab guides pick the TS-464.
 Can Synology NAS do Plex transcoding? The DS925+ and Synology's other AMD-based Plus models have no integrated GPU, so Plex cannot use hardware transcoding on them and every transcode runs in software on the CPU. Synology's Intel-based models, such as the DS225+, have Intel graphics that Plex can use with a Plex Pass. If your clients direct play, this matters little. For phones, browsers, and remote streams that need transcoding, an Intel-based QNAP such as the TS-464 is the safer choice.
 Is QNAP safe to use in 2026? Yes, if you keep QTS updated and keep it off the open internet. QNAP devices were the target of the DeadBolt ransomware campaign in 2022, which hit internet-exposed NAS running Photo Station, and QNAP rated its November 2025 fix for seven Pwn2Own 2025 flaws in QTS and QuTS hero as critical. Synology has shipped critical fixes too, including DSM and Synology Photos flaws from Pwn2Own 2024. For either brand, use a VPN or the vendor's relay service for remote access, enable automatic updates, and disable services you do not use.
 Did Synology remove the third-party drive restriction? Partly. Since DSM 7.3 (October 2025), Synology's 2025 Plus, Value and J models, such as the DS925+ and DS225+, accept third-party 3.5-inch HDDs and 2.5-inch SATA SSDs, but M.2 storage pools and cache still need drives on Synology's compatibility list. Synology still recommends drives from that list.

 How we judged the field
 We do not run our own storage lab. Instead we synthesize published reviews and aggregated owner reports to reach a verdict you can trust. For home NAS units in the 2-to-4-bay class, a handful of criteria consistently separate a great buy from a frustrating one.
 Transcoding ability: whether the processor can hardware-transcode 4K video for Plex, Jellyfin or Emby, which is the single biggest differentiator for media use.
 Networking: 2.5GbE is now the floor; 10GbE is the meaningful upgrade for editing large files over the network.
 Software maturity: how polished, reliable and well-supported the operating system and mobile apps are, which matters most for non-technical households.
 Expansion and memory: NVMe cache slots, memory headroom, and upgrade paths that keep the unit useful for years.
 Drive freedom and value: whether you can use the drives you want, and how much hardware you get for the money. Remember that all of these ship without drives.

 What to look for
 Match the CPU to your use: if you want Plex or Jellyfin to stream 4K, insist on an Intel chip with integrated graphics for hardware transcoding, and be wary of GPU-less processors.
 Treat 2.5GbE as the minimum, and consider 10GbE only if the rest of your network and your workflow can actually use it.
 Buy memory and NVMe headroom you can grow into; DDR5 and two cache slots age far better than fixed, soldered configurations.
 Check drive compatibility before you buy, and factor two to four drives into your budget since every unit here is sold diskless.
 Weigh software honestly: DSM is the safest bet for non-technical users, while UGOS, TOS and QTS reward buyers willing to learn a little more.
 Plan an off-site backup regardless of model; a NAS with redundancy protects against a dead drive, not against theft, fire or ransomware.

 Questions, answered
 Do these NAS devices come with hard drives? No. Every model here ships diskless, which is standard for this class. You buy two to four 3.5-inch SATA hard drives (or SSDs) separately and install them yourself. Budget for the drives as a meaningful part of the total cost, and where possible buy identical drives so a RAID array is balanced. This is general product information, not a recommendation for your specific setup; check each maker's current compatibility list before purchasing.
 How many bays do I actually need, two or four? A 2-bay unit in a mirrored configuration is plenty for backups and a photo vault, and it is cheaper and quieter. Choose a 4-bay model if you run a large, growing media library, want to stream several 4K files at once, or value more flexible expansion and redundancy. All four units reviewed here are four-bay, which is the sweet spot for a long-lived home server.
 Which of these is best for a Plex or Jellyfin media server? The UGREEN NASync DXP4800 Plus and TerraMaster F4-424 Pro are the strongest, because their Intel chips include integrated graphics that hardware-transcode 4K video efficiently. The Synology DS925+ is the weakest for this specific job: its AMD processor has no GPU and cannot hardware-transcode, so demanding 4K streams fall back to slower software transcoding.
 What is the Synology drive lock-in issue? Synology's 2025-generation units, including the DS925+, initially restricted full functionality to Synology-branded drives and a short approved list. After criticism, a DSM 7.3 update in late 2025 restored the ability to install the system and create storage pools on non-validated third-party drives on Plus, Value and J series models. Some friction and warning prompts can remain, so if you want maximum drive freedom, the other three brands are more open.
 Is a NAS worth it over a cloud subscription? For most households that store a lot of photos, video and backups, yes. A NAS is a one-time hardware cost (plus drives and electricity) rather than a recurring fee, keeps your data in your own home, and gives you far more space than typical cloud tiers. The trade-off is that you are responsible for setup, updates and an off-site backup copy, since a single NAS is not itself a complete backup strategy.
